Let $z$ be a primitive root of odd order $\ell>1$. Write $N=\ell N_1+N_0$ for $N\in\mathbb Z$ and $r=\ell r_1+r_0$ for $r\ge0$, with $0\le N_0,r_0<\ell$. The symmetric quantum binomial, interpreted by its Laurent-polynomial product for negative upper index, satisfies
$$\begin{bmatrix}N\\r\end{bmatrix}_z=\binom{N_1}{r_1}\begin{bmatrix}N_0\\r_0\end{bmatrix}_z.$$
For a specialized family $X^{(n)}$ with the divided-power multiplication of [[lem-divided-power-and-toral-quantum-binomial-reordering-identities]],
$$X^{(a\ell+r)}=\frac{(X^{(\ell)})^aX^r}{a![r]_z!}\qquad(a\ge0,\ 0\le r<\ell).$$
In particular the family is generated by $X$ and $X^{(\ell)}$; modulo the ideal generated by $X$, a divided power vanishes unless its index is divisible by $\ell$, and $X^{(a\ell)}=(X^{(\ell)})^a/a!$.

Take a finite-type semisimple Cartan datum with standard symmetrizers $d_i$, chosen weight lattice $Q_{\rm root}\subseteq P\subseteq P_{\rm full}$, dual lattice $P^\vee$, and $K_i=K_{d_ih_i}$. Specialize at a primitive root $\zeta$ of odd order $\ell>1$, with $\gcd(\ell,d_i)=1$ for all $i$, and put $z_i=\zeta^{d_i}$. In the actual specialized toral algebra, the quotient by all $K_h-1$ is the polynomial algebra on $H_i=T_{i,0,\ell}$. If $c=\ell c_1+c_0$ and $t=\ell t_1+t_0$, with residues in $[0,\ell-1]$, its exact formula is
$$T_{i,c,t}=\binom{H_i+c_1}{t_1}\begin{bmatrix}c_0\\t_0\end{bmatrix}_{z_i}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the integral triangular-decomposition supplier. The full form $U_A$ of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]], including every $T_{i,c,t}$, is stable under the library coproduct, counit, antipode and inverse antipode. Consequently every scalar specialization, including $U^L_\zeta$, is a Hopf algebra with bijective antipode. In the following formulas $a,b,r,t\ge0$, $c\in\mathbb Z$, and $q=q_i$, $K=K_i$ when the color is suppressed:

$$\Delta E_i^{(r)}=\sum_{a+b=r}q_i^{ab}E_i^{(a)}\otimes K_i^{-a}E_i^{(b)},\qquad \Delta F_i^{(r)}=\sum_{a+b=r}q_i^{-ab}F_i^{(a)}K_i^b\otimes F_i^{(b)}.$$

$$\Delta T_{i,c,t}=\sum_{a+b=t}q_i^{-bc}T_{i,c,a}K_i^{-b}\otimes K_i^aT_{i,0,b}.$$

$$S(E_i^{(r)})=(-1)^rq_i^{r(r-1)}E_i^{(r)}K_i^r,\qquad S(F_i^{(r)})=(-1)^rq_i^{-r(r-1)}K_i^{-r}F_i^{(r)}.$$

$$S(T_{i,c,t})=(-1)^tT_{i,t-c-1,t},\qquad \varepsilon(T_{i,c,t})=\begin{bmatrix}c\\t\end{bmatrix}_{q_i}.$$

The generalized Gaussian for integral $c$ denotes its Laurent-polynomial value; for $c=-b<0$ it equals $(-1)^t\begin{bmatrix}b+t-1\\t\end{bmatrix}_{q_i}$.

For distinct simple indices $i,j$, put $a=-a_{ij}\ge0$ and $v=q_i$. In the actual divided-power integral form, for $n,m\ge0$ and $m>an$,
$$\sum_{r+s=m}(-1)^rv^{r(an-m+1)}E_i^{(r)}E_j^{(n)}E_i^{(s)}=0.$$
The same identity holds with $E$ replaced by $F$. Since it is an equality of integral elements, it survives every specialization of the integral form, even when its divided-power indices have vanishing quantum factorials after specialization. This assertion does not assume a presentation theorem for that integral form.

Let $i\in I$ and let $T_{i,c,t}$ be the toral quantum binomials of
[[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]
($i\in I$, $c\in\mathbb Z$, $t\ge0$, $T_{i,c,0}=1$), inside the Drinfeld–Jimbo
algebra $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ of [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]
with $U_A$ and its parts $U_A^-,U_A^0,U_A^+$ as in that definition. Write
$E=E_i$, $F=F_i$, $E^{(a)}=E_i^{(a)}$, $F^{(b)}=F_i^{(b)}$ for the divided
powers of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]] and put
$q=q_i$ inside the displayed formulas.

(i) **Divided-power multiplication.** For all $a,b\ge0$,
$$E^{(a)}E^{(b)}=\binom{a+b}{a}_iE^{(a+b)},\qquad F^{(a)}F^{(b)}=\binom{a+b}{a}_iF^{(a+b)}.$$

(ii) **Toral recursion and commutation.** For $t\ge1$,
$$T_{i,c,t}=\frac{K_iq_i^{\,c-t+1}-K_i^{-1}q_i^{\,-c+t-1}}{q_i^{\,t}-q_i^{\,-t}}\,T_{i,c,t-1}.$$
Each $T_{i,c,t}$ is a Laurent polynomial in $K_i^{\pm1}$ with coefficients in
$\mathbb Q(q)$; the toral elements commute with one another and with all $K_h$.
For all $i,j$ and all $m\in\mathbb Z$ one has
$K_i^{\,m}T_{j,c,t}=T_{j,c,t}K_i^{\,m}$ if $i\ne j$, while
$E_iT_{i,c,t}=T_{i,c-2,t}E_i$, $E_jT_{i,c,t}=T_{i,c-a_{ij},t}E_j$,
$F_iT_{i,c,t}=T_{i,c+2,t}F_i$, $F_jT_{i,c,t}=T_{i,c+a_{ij},t}F_j$ for all $j$.
In particular $E_iT_{i,c,t}\in U_A^0E_i$, $F_iT_{i,c,t}\in U_A^0F_i$,
$T_{i,c,t}E_i=E_iT_{i,c+2,t}\in E_iU_A^0$ and
$T_{i,c,t}F_i=F_iT_{i,c-2,t}\in F_iU_A^0$: the toral factor can be moved to the
middle at the cost of a shift of the binomial index.

(iii) **Reordering identity.** For all $a,b\ge0$,
$$E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(b)}=\sum_{t=0}^{\min(a,b)}F_i^{(b-t)}\,T_{i,\,2t-a-b,\,t}\,E_i^{(a-t)},$$
with every coefficient a toral quantum binomial in $U_A^0$. In particular
$E_iF_i-F_iE_i=T_{i,0,1}$ and
$E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(a)}=\sum_{t=0}^{a}F_i^{(a-t)}T_{i,2t-2a,t}E_i^{(a-t)}$.
For $i\ne j$, $E_i^{(a)}$ and $F_j^{(b)}$ commute; the same-half divided powers
$E_i^{(a)},E_j^{(b)}$ (and likewise $F_i^{(a)},F_j^{(b)}$) commute whenever
$a_{ij}=0$, and for $a_{ij}\ne0$ no commutation is asserted.

(iv) **Triangular spanning.** Every element of $U_A$ is an $A$-linear
combination of products $b_-u\,b_+$ with $b_-\in U_A^-$, $u\in U_A^0$ and
$b_+\in U_A^+$; equivalently $U_A=U_A^-U_A^0U_A^+$ as an $A$-module. No
independence of the spanning family is asserted.

For every dominant label weight $\lambda$, let $V_A=U_Av_\lambda=U_A^-v_\lambda$ be the integral highest lattice inside the simple integrable module $L(\lambda)$, over $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$. Then each label-weight component of $V_A$ is finite free of rank $\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}L(\lambda)_\mu$, not merely torsionfree, and $V_A$ spans the field module. For every characteristic-zero field $k$ specialized at $q=1$, the fibre has the same weight dimensions and is the classical simple integrable highest weight module of the explicitly regularized realization, transported back to the original label lattice; hence its character is the Weyl–Kac character, the finite Weyl character in finite type. The integral quotient $U_A^-/\sum_i\sum_{s>\lambda(h_i)}U_A^-F_i^{(s)}$ is $V_A(\lambda)$; its field extension is $L(\lambda)$ in every symmetrizable type.

Let $\lambda\in P^+$, let $\pi_\lambda:U_q^-\to V(\lambda)$, $\pi_\lambda(P)=Pv_\lambda$, and let $G_\infty(b)$, $G_\lambda(\beta)$ be the lower global bases of $U_A^-$ and $V_A(\lambda)=U_A^-v_\lambda$ of [[def-lower-global-basis-of-a-quantum-highest-weight-module]]. Then:

(i) $\pi_\lambda:U_A^-\to V_A(\lambda)$ is a based quotient over $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$: $\pi_\lambda(G_\infty(b))=0$ if its crystal image $\pi_\lambda(b)\in\mathcal B(\lambda)\cup\{0\}$ is $0$, and $\pi_\lambda(G_\infty(b))=G_\lambda(\pi_\lambda(b))$ otherwise; consequently the kernel of $\pi_\lambda$ on $U_A^-$ is the $A$-span of exactly the killed lower global elements, the surviving elements map bijectively onto the integral highest-module basis $G_\lambda(\mathcal B(\lambda))$, the module weight components are finite free over $A$, and the compatible zero/infinity chart and residue projections have the crystal compatibility of the completed grand loop, all for every symmetrizable datum with the explicit label and auxiliary-realization convention;

(ii) more precisely, the integral kernel is
$$\ker\bigl(\pi_\lambda|_{U_A^-}\bigr)=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s>\lambda(h_i)}U_A^-F_i^{(s)}=\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(U_A^-\cap U_q^-F_i^{\lambda(h_i)+1}\bigr),$$
so the integral highest-module presentation uses all divided right powers beyond each highest limit, not just an ordinary power with a nonunit factorial.

Let $A=(a_{ij})$ be a finite-type Cartan matrix of size $r$
([[prop-finite-type-cartan-matrix-properties]]) and let $V$ be the complex
vector space with basis $e_1,\dots,e_r,f_1,\dots,f_r,h_1,\dots,h_r$. The
**Serre Lie algebra** $\mathfrak g(A)$ is the Lie algebra presented by the
generators $e_i,f_i,h_i$ and the relations
$$[h_i,h_j]=0,\qquad [h_i,e_j]=a_{ij}e_j,\qquad [h_i,f_j]=-a_{ij}f_j,\qquad [e_i,f_j]=\delta_{ij}h_i,$$
together with the **Serre relations**
$$(\operatorname{ad}e_i)^{1-a_{ij}}e_j=0,\qquad (\operatorname{ad}f_i)^{1-a_{ij}}f_j=0\qquad(i\ne j),$$
in the sense of [[def-lie-algebra-presented-by-generators-and-relations]].
The exponents are positive integers because $a_{ij}\le0$, and for $a_{ij}=0$
the Serre relations reduce to $[e_i,e_j]=0$ and $[f_i,f_j]=0$. The relations
express the standard presentation of a complex semisimple Lie algebra
relative to simple-root $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ triples; the algebra $\mathfrak g(A)$
is shown to be finite-dimensional semisimple with Cartan matrix $A$ in
[[thm-serre-presentation-theorem]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $A$ be a finite-type Cartan matrix of size
$r$, meaning the Cartan matrix of a based reduced crystallographic root system $\Phi(A)$ as in [[prop-finite-type-cartan-matrix-properties]], and let $\mathfrak g(A)$ be its Serre Lie algebra
([[def-serre-lie-algebra-of-a-finite-type-cartan-matrix]]). Then
$\mathfrak g(A)$ is finite-dimensional and semisimple, has a Cartan
subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ spanned by the images of the $h_i$, has root system
$\Phi(A)$ with Cartan matrix $A$, and has the triangular decomposition
$\mathfrak g(A)=\mathfrak n_-\oplus\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n_+$, where
$\mathfrak n_\pm$ is generated by the $e_i$ respectively $f_i$. If $r>0$ and $A$ is the
Cartan matrix of an irreducible root system, then $\mathfrak g(A)$ is simple. Conversely, if $\mathfrak g$ is a
finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with base
$\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r\}$ and root $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ triples
$(e_i,f_i,h_i)$ ([[thm-root-sl-two-triple]]), then the $e_i,f_i,h_i$ generate
$\mathfrak g$ and satisfy exactly the relations of
[[def-serre-lie-algebra-of-a-finite-type-cartan-matrix]], so that
$\mathfrak g\cong\mathfrak g(A)$.

For a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak a$, its **universal enveloping algebra** is $U(\mathfrak a)=T(\mathfrak a)/(xy-yx-[x,y])$, where $T$ is the algebra of finite linear combinations of finite tensor words, including the empty word $1$, and the denominator is the two-sided ideal generated by the displayed relations. For any ordered finite basis $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, the monomials $x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}$ form a vector-space basis of $U(\mathfrak a)$.

Now let $\mathfrak g$ be finite-dimensional complex semisimple with a Cartan and positive system as in the preceding root-structure lemma. Set $\mathfrak n^\pm=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi^\pm}\mathfrak g_\alpha$ and $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. For $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$ let $\mathbb C_\lambda$ be the one-dimensional $\mathfrak b$-module on which $\mathfrak h$ acts by $\lambda$ and $\mathfrak n^+$ by zero, and define $M(\lambda)=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b)}\mathbb C_\lambda$. It is generated by $v_\lambda=1\otimes1$, with $hv_\lambda=\lambda(h)v_\lambda$ and $\mathfrak n^+v_\lambda=0$, and is universal for these relations. Its negative-root ordered monomials on $v_\lambda$ form a basis; its support is $\lambda-Q_+$, each weight space is finite-dimensional and the top space has dimension one. It has a unique simple quotient $L(\lambda)$.

For every dominant integral $\lambda$, $L(\lambda)$ is finite-dimensional, its support is contained in $\lambda-Q_+$, its top weight has multiplicity one, and all its weight multiplicities are $W$-invariant. Every nonzero finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak g$-module is exactly one such $L(\lambda)$ up to isomorphism, with a unique dominant integral highest weight. These assertions include the zero algebra and use no AC.

Every finite-dimensional representation of a finite-dimensional semisimple
Lie algebra over any characteristic-zero field is completely reducible.

derivations.claim: By [F1], every divided power in $B$ vanishes unless its index is divisible by $\ell$, and the remaining ones are ordinary divided powers of $\bar e_i,\bar f_i$. Every toral generator is a polynomial in the $\bar H_i$, with its exact formula given in [F1]; further relations in $B$ are not yet excluded. Thus $\bar e_i,\bar f_i,\bar H_i$ generate $B$. In the complete mixed formula at exponents $\ell,\ell$, all intermediate contraction indices $0<t<\ell$ have remaining divided factors of nonzero residue and vanish in $B$. Its two surviving terms give $[\bar e_i,\bar f_i]=\bar H_i$; opposite colors commute. Iterating the toral shift through an $\ell$th divided power and using $T_{i,-\ell a_{ij},\ell}=H_i-a_{ij}$ gives $[\bar H_i,\bar e_j]=a_{ij}\bar e_j$ and $[\bar H_i,\bar f_j]=-a_{ij}\bar f_j$. The $\bar H_i$ commute.

For $i\ne j$, put $a=-a_{ij}$. Apply [F2] with $n=\ell$, $m=(a+1)\ell$. In $B$ only $r,s$ divisible by $\ell$ survive. For such $r$, $\zeta_i^{r(a\ell-(a+1)\ell+1)}=1$ and $(-1)^r=(-1)^{r/\ell}$ because $\ell$ is odd. By [F1] the resulting relation is $\sum_{b+c=a+1}(-1)^b\bar e_i^b\bar e_j\bar e_i^c/(b!c!)=0$, precisely the ordinary Serre relation after multiplying by $(a+1)!$. The negative relation is identical with $\bar f$ in place of $\bar e$. Thus [F4]'s Serre presentation and step 1.1 give a surjective homomorphism $\psi:U(\mathfrak g)\to B$. No presentation theorem for the divided-power specialization has been assumed.

Fix any dominant $\mu\in P$ and specialize the actual lattice $V_A(\ell\mu)$ of [F3] at $q=\zeta$. Finite freeness gives a finite-dimensional module with a nonzero rank-one top weight and its actual integral weight decomposition; the highest vector still generates it, since $V_A=U_A^-v$. The toral character of a weight $
u$ has $K_i$ value $\zeta_i^{
u(h_i)}$ and $H_i$ value $\lfloor
u(h_i)/\ellfloor$, by [F1] including negative upper indices. These values determine each integer $
u(h_i)$: the first gives its residue and the second its quotient. Since simple coroot coordinates distinguish weights in a semisimple lattice, the full toral characters of distinct weights are distinct. Finite polynomial interpolation in commuting toral operators therefore projects onto each actual weight space and preserves every submodule. A simple quotient $M$ of this finite-dimensional cyclic module exists by choosing a proper submodule of maximal dimension. It retains a nonzero top vector $v$ of weight $\ell\mu$, since a submodule containing $v$ would be the entire module; it also retains the weight decomposition and toral characters.

Every positive divided power kills $v$. For every $i$, also $F_iv=0$. Indeed for $j\ne i$ the positive $j$th divided powers commute past $F_i$ and kill it on $v$. For color $i$, the complete mixed reordering gives $E_i^{(r)}F_iv=0$ for $r>1$, since the possible contraction has right factor $E_i^{(r-1)}v=0$; at $r=1$ its coefficient is $[\ell\mu(h_i)]_{\zeta_i}=0$. Hence, if $F_iv$ were nonzero, it would be a highest-weight vector of weight $\ell\mu-\alpha_i$. Triangular spanning then puts its entire generated submodule in weights at most this weight, so it misses the original top weight and is proper. Simplicity of $M$ excludes this. Thus all small generators $E_i,F_i$ kill $v$.

Let $N\subseteq M$ be the common kernel of all $E_i,F_i$. It contains $v$. It is a sum of actual weight spaces: each small operator shifts the actual weight by its simple root, and distinct input weights give distinct output weights. Since the torus acts diagonally on those spaces, $N$ is toral-stable. It is also stable under every $E_i^{(\ell)},F_i^{(\ell)}$. For same-sign distinct colors, the good-order assumptions give $\ell>-a_{ij}$: finite-type off-diagonal entries have absolute values at most $3$, odd order is at least $3$, and the only possible equality $3$ in $G_2$ is excluded by $3\nmid\ell$. Apply [F2] with $n=1,m=\ell$ to a vector of $N$. Its $r=0$ term is $E_jE_i^{(\ell)}$ applied to that vector; the $r=\ell$ term has rightmost $E_j$, and every intermediate term has rightmost $E_i^{(s)}$ with $0<s<\ell$. These all vanish by [F1], leaving the desired zero; the negative proof is identical. Same-color same-sign operators commute. Opposite distinct colors commute. For opposite signs in the same color, mixed reordering gives an error factor of degree $\ell-1$, which vanishes on $N$ after its toral factor acts diagonally; hence these small operators also annihilate the image of $N$ under the big divided generator. Finally [F1] generates all divided powers from the small and big generators. Thus $N$ is a full submodule, and simplicity yields $N=M$.

The cyclic module $M$ is now generated from $v$ by big divided generators and the torus alone, so all its weights differ from $\ell\mu$ by multiples of $\ell$ times roots. Every $K_h$ therefore acts as $1$, and step 5.1 shows that $J$ kills $M$. Along $\psi$, it is a finite-dimensional simple classical module, since $\psi$ is onto, with highest vector $v$ and $\bar H_i v=\mu(h_i)v$ by [F1]. Classification in [F4] identifies it with $L(\mu)$. Consequently every classical dominant simple with highest weight in $P$ occurs as a $\psi$-pullback. This does not assert simplicity of the specialized Weyl module before taking its quotient.

These classical modules separate $U(\mathfrak g)$. For completeness, set $V=\mathfrak g$ and let $\rho:\mathfrak g\to\operatorname{End}(V)$ be its faithful adjoint representation; semisimplicity makes its kernel the zero center. On the polynomial algebra of the matrix space $\operatorname{End}(V)$, define the linear vector field $D_x$ by $D_x(M)=M\rho(x)$. On coordinate functions its bracket is $[D_x,D_y](M)=M[\rho(x),\rho(y)]$, so this is a Lie representation and extends to $U(\mathfrak g)$. If $u\ne0$ has PBW degree $m$, its top symbol is nonzero in $\operatorname{Sym}^m\mathfrak g$ by [F4]. At the identity matrix the principal symbol of $D_u$ is its image under $\operatorname{Sym}^m\rho$, which is injective because $\rho$ is injective and a finite basis of its image extends to a basis of the matrix space. Choose a homogeneous degree-$m$ polynomial in the shifted matrix coordinates, paired nontrivially with this symbol. Its lower derivatives vanish at the identity, so $D_up$ has nonzero value there. Thus $u$ acts nontrivially on this polynomial representation.

Polynomials of bounded total degree form finite-dimensional stable subspaces for these linear vector fields. By [F4] each decomposes into classical simples. All its weights lie in the root lattice: the adjoint weights, their duals and their tensor or symmetric powers have this property. Hence every highest weight of these constituents belongs to $Q_{\rm root}\subseteq P$. If an element killed every simple supplied by step 6.1, it would kill every finite polynomial subspace and hence the entire polynomial representation, contradicting step 7.1. The intersection of their annihilators is therefore zero. Since $\ker\psi$ annihilates all of them, $\psi$ is injective and hence an isomorphism. If $\mathfrak g=0$, $U(\mathfrak g)=\mathbb C$ acts faithfully on the constant polynomial module, giving the same conclusion directly.

Compose the quotient map $U^L_\zeta\to B$ with $\psi^{-1}$. This constructs a surjective algebra map with exact kernel $J$. Its divided-power values follow from [F1], and its toral values follow from the toral quotient formula there. These formulas cover every generator of the actual integral form, so the map is unique. In particular this construction proves well-definedness on all relations of the actual specialized subalgebra, rather than checking only a possibly incomplete proposed list of divided-power relations.

The actual root Hopf structure in [F1] makes $J$ a Hopf ideal. On its generators, $\Delta(E_i)$ and $\Delta(F_i)$ lie in $J\otimes U+U\otimes J$; $\Delta(K_h-1)=(K_h-1)\otimes K_h+1\otimes(K_h-1)$; and counit and antipode preserve their ideal. In $B$, the interior terms of the divided-power coproduct of $E_i^{(\ell)},F_i^{(\ell)}$ vanish by [F1], and $K_h=1$, so $\bar e_i,\bar f_i$ are primitive. Their commutators $\bar H_i$ are primitive as well. Therefore $\psi$ preserves the usual classical Hopf maps on all its generating Lie elements and is a Hopf isomorphism. Its inverse composed with the quotient is the claimed Hopf Frobenius map. The inherited Choice assumptions are exactly [C1]; no rank-one restriction, integral-presentation shortcut, or unidentified small-quantum-group kernel was used.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the integral triangular-decomposition supplier. The full form $U_A$ of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]], including every $T_{i,c,t}$, is stable under the library coproduct, counit, antipode and inverse antipode. Consequently every scalar specialization, including $U^L_\zeta$, is a Hopf algebra with bijective antipode. In the following formulas $a,b,r,t\ge0$, $c\in\mathbb Z$, and $q=q_i$, $K=K_i$ when the color is suppressed:

$$\Delta E_i^{(r)}=\sum_{a+b=r}q_i^{ab}E_i^{(a)}\otimes K_i^{-a}E_i^{(b)},\qquad \Delta F_i^{(r)}=\sum_{a+b=r}q_i^{-ab}F_i^{(a)}K_i^b\otimes F_i^{(b)}.$$

$$\Delta T_{i,c,t}=\sum_{a+b=t}q_i^{-bc}T_{i,c,a}K_i^{-b}\otimes K_i^aT_{i,0,b}.$$

$$S(E_i^{(r)})=(-1)^rq_i^{r(r-1)}E_i^{(r)}K_i^r,\qquad S(F_i^{(r)})=(-1)^rq_i^{-r(r-1)}K_i^{-r}F_i^{(r)}.$$

$$S(T_{i,c,t})=(-1)^tT_{i,t-c-1,t},\qquad \varepsilon(T_{i,c,t})=\begin{bmatrix}c\\t\end{bmatrix}_{q_i}.$$

The generalized Gaussian for integral $c$ denotes its Laurent-polynomial value; for $c=-b<0$ it equals $(-1)^t\begin{bmatrix}b+t-1\\t\end{bmatrix}_{q_i}$.

In the same positive-first/negative-second completion $\widehat C$ of [[def-root-height-completion-for-weightwise-quasi-r-intertwiners]], let $\Theta=\sum_\nu\Theta_\nu$ be the unique normalized bar-coproduct intertwiner of [[thm-the-weightwise-quasi-r-intertwiner-exists-and-is-unique]]. Then:

(i) $\Theta^{-1}=\overline\Theta=(\psi\otimes\psi)(\Theta)$, the inverse being taken in the root-height convolution algebra of $\widehat C$ and not switching the positive and negative tensor order;

(ii) for every $\nu$ the exact threefold identities hold:
$$(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Theta_\nu=\sum_{\gamma+\eta=\nu}(\Theta_\gamma)_{23}(1\otimes K_{-\eta}\otimes1)(\Theta_\eta)_{13},$$
$$(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\Theta_\nu=\sum_{\gamma+\eta=\nu}(\Theta_\gamma)_{12}(1\otimes K_\eta\otimes1)(\Theta_\eta)_{13},$$
with subscripts denoting tensor positions and $\Theta_{\nu'}=0$ when $\nu'\notin Q_+$;

(iii) the two normalized tensor-bar compositions satisfy the field cocycle identity
$$((\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Theta)\Theta_{12}=((\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\Theta)\Theta_{23},$$
coefficientwise in the transported source completion and on every vector for which the iterated actions are finite;

(iv) the bar-coproduct counterpart needed for the cocycle is
$$(\mathrm{id}\otimes\overline\Delta)\Theta_\nu=\sum_{\gamma+\eta=\nu}(\Theta_\gamma)_{13}(1\otimes K_{-\gamma}\otimes1)(\Theta_\eta)_{12}.$$

Removing the normalization $\Theta_0=1$ permits arbitrary scalar multiples of the same linear intertwiner equation, so normalization is essential for uniqueness; no integrality of coefficients and no uncontrolled infinite evaluation is asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For $M\in\mathcal C_\zeta$ of [[def-full-toral-weight-root-of-unity-module-category]], $\dim M_\mu=\dim M_{s_i\mu}$ for every simple reflection $s_i$. Consequently its formal weight character is Weyl invariant. If a nonzero weight vector $v\in M_\lambda$ is killed by every $E_i^{(s)}$ for $s>0$, then $n_i=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$ and $F_i^{(r)}v=0$ for every $r>n_i$. These assertions concern the full divided-power action, including powers whose index is at least $\ell$.

derivations.claim: Use [F1] to define $x(m\otimes n)=\Delta(x)(m\otimes n)$, with the vector-space associator and unit constraints. Every summand of a divided coproduct has the required sum-weight shift. Evaluating its toral-binomial coproduct on $M_\lambda\otimes N_\mu$ gives the Gaussian Vandermonde sum $\begin{bmatrix}\langle\lambda+\mu,h_i\rangle+c\\t\end{bmatrix}_\zeta$, so the tensor product has the full required toral weights. The counit gives weight zero on the unit, since $\varepsilon(T_{i,c,t})=\begin{bmatrix}c\\t\end{bmatrix}_\zeta$. Hopf coassociativity and the counit equations prove that the vector-space constraints are module maps and satisfy coherence. Kernels and cokernels of weight-preserving maps inherit the same scalar toral and shift identities; direct sums do also. The full toral characters separate the integer labels: writing $n=a\ell+b$, $0\le b<\ell$, the root Gaussian block identity gives $\begin{bmatrix}n\\\ell\end{bmatrix}_\zeta=\zeta^{\ell(n-\ell)}a$. Indeed express the symmetric Gaussian as $q^{\ell(n-\ell)}$ times the ordinary Gaussian at $q^{-2}$ and take the degree-$\ell$ coefficient in the length-$\ell$ blocks of its generating product; for negative $n$ the inverse product gives the same integer $a$. The eigenvalue of $K_i$ determines $b$ and the displayed sign factor, and the binomial eigenvalue then determines $a$. Since the simple coroots distinguish full $P$-weights, every algebra module map automatically preserves weights. Thus the category is also a full subcategory of the module category. Therefore it is linear and abelian, and the tensor product stays in it.

We first justify specialization of the completed identities for all integral generators, rather than deducing higher identities from ordinary generators at the root. By [F2] every $\Theta_\nu$ has integral algebra coefficients. Since $\psi$ preserves the divided powers, toral group elements and binomials (indeed $\psi(T_{i,c,t})=T_{i,c,t}$), its bar also has integral coefficients. For each individual $u=E_i^{(r)},F_i^{(r)},K_h,T_{i,c,t}$, both sides of the generic identity in [F3] have, in each bi-root-degree, finitely many terms in $U_A\otimes_AU_A$: the coproduct of $u$ is finite by [F1] and its possible root degrees are finite. The two sides are equal in the generic tensor square, so [F4] makes them equal already over $A$. The same argument in the free triple tensor product treats both factorizations in [F3], and the inverse convolution identities have only finitely many decompositions of each positive root degree. Consequently all these identities specialize at $q=\zeta$. This proves specialized intertwining for the higher divided powers independently, without dividing by $[r]_\zeta!$ or requiring a generic lift of any module.

On $M^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(M,\mathbb C)$ give the left action $(xf)(m)=f(S(x)m)$ and set $(M^*)_{-\lambda}=(M_\lambda)^*$. The antipode formulas in [F1] give precisely the divided-power shifts, while $S(T_{i,c,t})=(-1)^tT_{i,t-c-1,t}$ acts on the $\lambda$-dual line by $(-1)^t\begin{bmatrix}\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle+t-c-1\\t\end{bmatrix}_\zeta=\begin{bmatrix}-\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle+c\\t\end{bmatrix}_\zeta$. Thus the dual has the full toral weights. Evaluation $f\otimes m\mapsto f(m)$ and coevaluation $1\mapsto\sum_am_a\otimes m^a$ are module maps by the two antipode equations; the latter tensor is independent of the chosen basis because it corresponds to the identity linear map. Their composites are the identity by finite dual-basis contraction. Using the bijective $S^{-1}$ gives right duals and the other triangles, with the same weight check. This proves rigidity.

These completed identities can actually be evaluated here. For any pair of finite weight sets, $\Theta_
u$ can act on $M_\lambda\otimes N_\mu$ only if $\lambda+
u$ and $\mu-
u$ are in their respective finite supports. There are finitely many such $
u$. Iterated products and coproduct actions on any fixed finite tensor product are finite as well: all intermediate weights lie in finite supports, so each successive transfer has only finitely many possible degrees. The same statement holds after an integral generator is applied, since its coproduct is finite. Thus the coefficientwise specialized equalities in step 1.2 become actual equalities of linear maps. In particular $\Theta^{-1}$ is the finite operator obtained from its integral inverse coefficients.

The bicharacter supplies the missing toral part of $R$. Work first with $q=z^D$ and the generic phase $z^{D(\lambda,\mu)}$; specialize $z$ to the chosen $t$ only after the following weight identities. For $m_\lambda\otimes n_\mu$, $D(E_i\otimes1)D^{-1}=E_i\otimes K_i$ and $D(1\otimes E_i)D^{-1}=K_i\otimes E_i$, because $(\alpha_i,\mu)=\langle\mu,h_i\rangle$; replacing $E_i$ by $F_i$ reverses the toral exponents. Hence $D\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}(E_i)D^{-1}=\overline\Delta(E_i)$ and likewise for $F_i$. For every divided power this can be checked without generic division: the term $q^{ab}K_i^{-a}E_i^{(b)}\otimes E_i^{(a)}$ of $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}E_i^{(r)}$, $a+b=r$, acquires the bicharacter ratio $q^{b\langle\mu,h_i\rangle+a\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle+2ab}$; the first toral action contributes $q^{-a(\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle+2b)}$. Reordering the resulting second factor gives the operator $q^{-ab}E_i^{(b)}\otimes K_i^bE_i^{(a)}$, the corresponding term of $\overline\Delta E_i^{(r)}$. Similarly the term $q^{-ab}F_i^{(b)}\otimes F_i^{(a)}K_i^b$ acquires the ratio $q^{-b\langle\mu,h_i\rangle-a\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle+2ab}$; including the second toral action leaves $q^{ab}F_i^{(b)}K_i^{-a}\otimes F_i^{(a)}$, exactly the term of $\overline\Delta F_i^{(r)}$. These computations involve Laurent units only and hold directly at $q=\zeta$ for every $r$. For a toral binomial, $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}(T)$ and $\overline\Delta(T)$ have the identical scalar $\begin{bmatrix}\langle\lambda+\mu,h_i\rangle+c\\t\end{bmatrix}_\zeta$, so their equality is checked directly; the same holds for $K_h$. We obtain $D\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}(u)=\overline\Delta(u)D$ for every full integral generator at the root. Combining this with step 1.2 gives $\Delta(u)B=B\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}(u)$ for $B=\Theta D$, hence $R\Delta(u)=\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}(u)R$ for $R=B^{-1}=D^{-1}\Theta^{-1}$.

Let $\rho^\vee$ be the half sum of positive coroots. Then $2\rho^\vee\in Q^\vee$ and $\langle\alpha_i,\rho^\vee\rangle=1$. By [F1], $S^2(E_i^{(r)})=\zeta^{-2r}E_i^{(r)}$, $S^2(F_i^{(r)})=\zeta^{2r}F_i^{(r)}$, while $S^2$ fixes the torus and binomials. These are precisely conjugation by $g=K_{-2\rho^\vee}$, so $S^2(x)=gxg^{-1}$ for every full generator and hence the full algebra. The double-dual action on the canonical vector-space bidual $\jmath(v)$ is $x\jmath(v)=\jmath(S^2(x)v)$. It follows that $j(v)=\jmath(gv)$ is a module isomorphism. It is natural; since $g$ is grouplike it is monoidal and is the identity on the unit. It is therefore a pivotal structure in the sense of [[def-pivotal-structure]].

Here are both hexagon identities, beyond the tensor-bar cocycle. On three weight factors the bicharacter gives $(\Delta\otimes\operatorname{id})D=D_{13}D_{23}$ and $(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)D=D_{12}D_{13}$. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

derivations.claim: Evaluate the finite character identity in [F1] at $e^\mu=q^{(2\rho,\mu)}$. Symmetry of the invariant form and changing $w$ to $w^{-1}$ show that its alternating numerator equals $\sum_w\det(w)q^{(2w\rho,\lambda+\rho)}$. Evaluate the Weyl denominator identity instead at $e^\mu=q^{2(\mu,\lambda+\rho)}$; this gives the numerator product $\prod_{\alpha>0}(q^{(\lambda+\rho,\alpha)}-q^{-(\lambda+\rho,\alpha)})$, since $\sum_{\alpha>0}\alpha=2\rho$. The denominator is the same product with $\lambda=0$. Thus the character specialization is the quotient of these two products as a rational function, or equivalently their cross-multiplied Laurent-polynomial identity. Replacing $q$ by $q^{-1}$ changes neither the quotient nor the quantum-integer factors, so it is also the character evaluated at $e^\mu=q^{-(2\rho,\mu)}$.

Every positive-root height $\langle\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle$ lies between one and $h-1$, strictly below $\ell$. Since $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta^2)=\ell$, a quantum integer $[n]_\zeta$ vanishes exactly when $\ell$ divides $n$; also $\zeta-\zeta^{-1}\ne0$. The denominator in step 1.1 is therefore nonzero after specializing, so ordinary scalar division is now justified. By [F2] its value is the quantum dimension, proving the formula with no singular evaluation of a formal quotient.

A finite simple reflection permutes positive roots except for reversing its own simple root; invariance of the form shows that the numerator product changes sign under the dot action of that reflection. These reflections generate $W$, yielding finite Weyl alternation. A translation $\lambda\mapsto\lambda+\ell\beta$ with $\beta\in Q$ multiplies each numerator factor by $\zeta^{\ell(\beta,\alpha)}$, because $\zeta^\ell$ is one or minus one. The full multiplier is $\zeta^{\ell(\beta,2\rho)}=1$: write $\beta=\sum n_i\alpha_i$ and use $(\alpha_i,\rho)=1$ to get $(\beta,2\rho)=2\sum n_i$. Therefore the product is $\ell Q$-periodic. Together these give the affine sign relation. A numerator factor vanishes exactly when $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\ell\mathbb Z$, namely an affine reflection wall. In the open bottom alcove every such integer lies strictly between zero and $\ell$, so none vanishes.

Trace is additive over an invariant-subspace exact sequence: choose a weight-adapted basis and use the block triangular action of $g$. Hence quantum dimension adds along any Weyl filtration. If every section label is affine singular, step 3.1 makes each of its quantum dimensions zero, so their sum is zero. These conclusions are all that has been asserted about tilting dimensions here; cancellation for nonsingular labels outside the alcove requires a separate argument.

Let $\zeta\in\mathbb C^\times$ satisfy $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta^2)=\ell$, with $\ell$ odd and $\ell>h$, where $h$ is the Coxeter number. Both orders $\ell$ and $2\ell$ for $\zeta$ are permitted. Work in the category of finite dimensional integrable type-1 modules with full toral quantum-binomial weight characters supplied by [[thm-root-of-unity-lusztig-module-category-is-braided-rigid]], not just eigenvalues of the $K_i$.

For $\lambda\in P^+$ let $V_A(\lambda)=U_A^-v_\lambda$ be the actual finite free highest lattice of [[thm-quantum-highest-weight-modules-deform-the-classical-weight-character]]. Define
$$
\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)=\mathbb C\otimes_{A,\,v\mapsto\zeta}V_A(\lambda),\qquad \nabla_\zeta(\lambda)=\Delta_\zeta(-w_0\lambda)^*.
$$
Here $(-)^*$ is the ordinary finite-dimensional Hopf dual in the stated category. These are the **Weyl** and **dual Weyl** families. The pivotal isomorphism identifies their double duals with the original modules, so ordinary duality exchanges the two families, with label $\lambda\mapsto-w_0\lambda$.

A module has a Weyl or dual Weyl filtration if it has a finite submodule filtration with sections in the corresponding family. A **tilting module** has both filtrations. Existence of indecomposable tiltings at every label, their classification, and their affine-alcove behavior are separate results; these are not included in this definition.

Under [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$ is a nonzero finite dimensional integrable type-1 module, cyclic on a highest vector of label $\lambda$ with one-dimensional highest space. Its formal character is the classical finite Weyl character $\chi_\lambda$. It is universal among finite dimensional highest-label modules generated by a vector of label $\lambda$. It has a unique maximal proper submodule and unique simple head $L_\zeta(\lambda)$. The simple heads are pairwise nonisomorphic and exhaust finite dimensional simple type-1 modules. The dual Weyl module has the same character, unique simple socle $L_\zeta(\lambda)$, and weights at most $\lambda$.

These assertions use the inherited Axiom of Choice. They do not assert root-specialized semisimplicity or that these Weyl modules are simple.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The finite tensor lattice $V_A(\lambda)\otimes_A V_A(\mu)$ has the constructed finite based global basis by [F1], with exactly this underlying integral lattice. Apply [F2] before specializing; every section is an integral highest lattice and every quotient is free. Its specialization is therefore a genuine Weyl filtration of $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)\otimes\Delta_\zeta(\mu)$ with all submodule injections intact. This proof uses an integral filtration and never specializes a generic direct-sum decomposition.

Let $M,N$ have Weyl filtrations. Tensor a filtration of $M$ with $N$; exactness gives sections $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)\otimes N$. Tensor each filtration of $N$ with this Weyl factor and use step 1.1 to give each of its sections a Weyl filtration. Pull these finite filtrations back through the successive quotient maps to refine the original filtration. This produces a finite Weyl filtration of $M\otimes N$. The zero case has the empty filtration.

If $M,N$ are dual-Weyl-filtered, then $M^*,N^*$ are Weyl-filtered by [F3]. Step 2.1 makes $N^*\otimes M^*$ Weyl-filtered; its dual is dual-Weyl-filtered and is isomorphic to $M\otimes N$ by the dual tensor isomorphism and the pivotal double-dual identifications. Thus dual Weyl filtrations are tensor stable as well. Ordinary duality exchanges the two filtration kinds, so it preserves their intersection. Concatenating filtrations proves finite-sum closure. The trivial one-dimensional module is both $\Delta_\zeta(0)$ and $\nabla_\zeta(0)$, hence is tilting. These arguments prove exactly the asserted tensor, dual, sum and unit statements.

citations.quote:
Under [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$ is a nonzero finite dimensional integrable type-1 module, cyclic on a highest vector of label $\lambda$ with one-dimensional highest space. Its formal character is the classical finite Weyl character $\chi_\lambda$. It is universal among finite dimensional highest-label modules generated by a vector of label $\lambda$. It has a unique maximal proper submodule and unique simple head $L_\zeta(\lambda)$. The simple heads are pairwise nonisomorphic and exhaust finite dimensional simple type-1 modules. The dual Weyl module has the same character, unique simple socle $L_\zeta(\lambda)$, and weights at most $\lambda$.

These assertions use the inherited Axiom of Choice. They do not assert root-specialized semisimplicity or that these Weyl modules are simple.

Under [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], and the inherited Axiom of Choice, the tensor product of two Weyl-filtered modules is Weyl-filtered, and the tensor product of two dual-Weyl-filtered modules is dual-Weyl-filtered. Hence tilting modules are closed under tensor products, ordinary duals and finite direct sums, and contain the tensor unit. This theorem does not presume direct-summand closure or classify indecomposable tiltings.

derivations.claim: If a finite module $V$ has no label strictly greater than $\lambda$, every surjection $V\to\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$ splits: lift its highest vector to a label-$\lambda$ vector $v\in V$. All positive divided powers kill $v$ because they would increase its label strictly. The universal property in [F1] extends the highest-vector lift to a module map from $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$, and its composite with the surjection fixes the highest generator, hence is the identity. This argument permits labels incomparable with $\lambda$ in $V$.

A nonzero map $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)\to\nabla_\zeta(\mu)$ has image containing the unique simple socle $L_\zeta(\mu)$: every nonzero finite-length submodule contains a simple submodule, and this socle is unique. Its weights are at most $\lambda$, so $\mu\le\lambda$. On the other hand the highest generator has label $\lambda$ in the target, so $\lambda\le\mu$. Thus $\lambda=\mu$. At equal labels the image of the highest line is an arbitrary scalar multiple of the unique highest line, which lies in the simple socle; its generated image is precisely that socle. This gives a one-dimensional Hom space, and the map is the simple-head quotient followed by socle inclusion.

If $M$ is Weyl-filtered and $\lambda$ is a maximal support label, the canonical action map $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)\otimes_{\mathbb C} M_\lambda\to M$ is injective and its quotient is Weyl-filtered with no section of label $\lambda$. To prove this, induct along a chosen Weyl filtration. If its final section has label $\lambda$, the short exact sequence splits by step 1.1; the trace acquires exactly this additional copy. If its final section has different label $\gamma$, it has no $\lambda$ weight, since otherwise $\lambda\le\gamma$ would contradict maximality and distinctness. Thus $M_\lambda$ and its generated trace are contained in the preceding flag subobject, where induction applies, and the quotient extends by $\Delta_\zeta(\gamma)$. This proves the claim in both cases; it also identifies the submodule canonically, independently of the chosen filtration.

Consider an extension $0\to\nabla_\zeta(\mu)\to V\to\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)\to0$. If $\lambda\not<\mu$, no weight of $V$ is strictly greater than $\lambda$, since such a weight would lie at most $\mu$ and force $\lambda<\mu$. Thus it splits by step 1.1. If $\lambda<\mu$, dualizing produces an extension with Weyl quotient of label $\mu^*$ and dual Weyl kernel of label $\lambda^*$. The involution $-w_0$ preserves the dominance order, so $\lambda^*<\mu^*$, and the already settled case splits this dual extension. Exact involutive duality then splits the original extension. Therefore all standard-costandard degree-one extension groups vanish. Inducting on a Weyl filtration in the first variable and a dual Weyl filtration in the second variable, using the Hom-extension exact sequences (equivalently pullback and pushout of short exact sequences), proves that every extension of a Weyl-filtered module by a dual-Weyl-filtered module splits.

Suppose $M=Q\oplus R$ is Weyl-filtered. Its canonical maximal trace from step 2.1 is stable under the two projection idempotents, since it is generated by $M_\lambda$; the restrictions to this trace are the identity on the Weyl factor tensored with the corresponding projections of $M_\lambda$. Hence its intersections with $Q,R$ are respectively $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)\otimes Q_\lambda$ and $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)\otimes R_\lambda$. The quotient decomposes as the direct sum of $Q$ and $R$ modulo these intersections, and is Weyl-filtered of smaller total dimension. Induction on total dimension therefore gives Weyl filtrations of these two quotients, and adjoining the respective Weyl traces gives Weyl filtrations of $Q,R$. The base $M=0$ is immediate. Exact duality proves the same for dual Weyl flags, hence for tiltings. Any finite dimensional module splits into indecomposables by repeatedly decomposing a decomposable summand, since positive dimensions decrease; the established summand closure makes each resulting tilting summand tilting.

For a sufficiently high power of any endomorphism $a$ of a finite dimensional module, kernel and image stabilize and give the module decomposition $T=\ker a^n\oplus\operatorname{im}a^n$. For an indecomposable $T$, every endomorphism is therefore nilpotent or invertible. The maximal-trace proof in step 2.1 also works simultaneously for the finite set $\Gamma$ of all maximal support labels: the corresponding Weyl sections split past one another by step 1.1, and their sum is the injected submodule $S=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Gamma}\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)\otimes T_\lambda$ with Weyl-filtered quotient. If the total dimension of $\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Gamma}T_\lambda$ exceeded one, define a homomorphism $S\to T$ fixing one selected highest basis line and killing another, by acting on the displayed multiplicity spaces. step 2.2 extends this map to an endomorphism of $T$ because its cokernel is Weyl-filtered. That endomorphism fixes a nonzero vector and kills another, so it is neither nilpotent nor invertible, a contradiction. Thus an indecomposable tilting has a unique maximal label and a one-dimensional highest space.

Let $T,T'$ be indecomposable tiltings and $\lambda$ their common maximal label. step 2.1 supplies inclusions of a copy of $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$ into each, with Weyl-filtered cokernels. step 2.2 extends the common highest-line identification to homomorphisms $f:T\to T'$ and $g:T'\to T$, whose composites fix that line. By step 3.2 these composites are not nilpotent and hence are invertible. Therefore $f$ is an isomorphism. This proves the claimed uniqueness of indecomposable tiltings at each label where one exists, without asserting existence at the remaining labels.

Let $\lambda\in P^+$, let $\pi_\lambda:U_q^-\to V(\lambda)$, $\pi_\lambda(P)=Pv_\lambda$, and let $G_\infty(b)$, $G_\lambda(\beta)$ be the lower global bases of $U_A^-$ and $V_A(\lambda)=U_A^-v_\lambda$ of [[def-lower-global-basis-of-a-quantum-highest-weight-module]]. Then:

(i) $\pi_\lambda:U_A^-\to V_A(\lambda)$ is a based quotient over $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$: $\pi_\lambda(G_\infty(b))=0$ if its crystal image $\pi_\lambda(b)\in\mathcal B(\lambda)\cup\{0\}$ is $0$, and $\pi_\lambda(G_\infty(b))=G_\lambda(\pi_\lambda(b))$ otherwise; consequently the kernel of $\pi_\lambda$ on $U_A^-$ is the $A$-span of exactly the killed lower global elements, the surviving elements map bijectively onto the integral highest-module basis $G_\lambda(\mathcal B(\lambda))$, the module weight components are finite free over $A$, and the compatible zero/infinity chart and residue projections have the crystal compatibility of the completed grand loop, all for every symmetrizable datum with the explicit label and auxiliary-realization convention;

(ii) more precisely, the integral kernel is
$$\ker\bigl(\pi_\lambda|_{U_A^-}\bigr)=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s>\lambda(h_i)}U_A^-F_i^{(s)}=\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(U_A^-\cap U_q^-F_i^{\lambda(h_i)+1}\bigr),$$
so the integral highest-module presentation uses all divided right powers beyond each highest limit, not just an ordinary power with a nonunit factorial.

Let $i\in I$ and let $T_{i,c,t}$ be the toral quantum binomials of
[[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]
($i\in I$, $c\in\mathbb Z$, $t\ge0$, $T_{i,c,0}=1$), inside the Drinfeld–Jimbo
algebra $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ of [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]
with $U_A$ and its parts $U_A^-,U_A^0,U_A^+$ as in that definition. Write
$E=E_i$, $F=F_i$, $E^{(a)}=E_i^{(a)}$, $F^{(b)}=F_i^{(b)}$ for the divided
powers of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]] and put
$q=q_i$ inside the displayed formulas.

(i) **Divided-power multiplication.** For all $a,b\ge0$,
$$E^{(a)}E^{(b)}=\binom{a+b}{a}_iE^{(a+b)},\qquad F^{(a)}F^{(b)}=\binom{a+b}{a}_iF^{(a+b)}.$$

(ii) **Toral recursion and commutation.** For $t\ge1$,
$$T_{i,c,t}=\frac{K_iq_i^{\,c-t+1}-K_i^{-1}q_i^{\,-c+t-1}}{q_i^{\,t}-q_i^{\,-t}}\,T_{i,c,t-1}.$$
Each $T_{i,c,t}$ is a Laurent polynomial in $K_i^{\pm1}$ with coefficients in
$\mathbb Q(q)$; the toral elements commute with one another and with all $K_h$.
For all $i,j$ and all $m\in\mathbb Z$ one has
$K_i^{\,m}T_{j,c,t}=T_{j,c,t}K_i^{\,m}$ if $i\ne j$, while
$E_iT_{i,c,t}=T_{i,c-2,t}E_i$, $E_jT_{i,c,t}=T_{i,c-a_{ij},t}E_j$,
$F_iT_{i,c,t}=T_{i,c+2,t}F_i$, $F_jT_{i,c,t}=T_{i,c+a_{ij},t}F_j$ for all $j$.
In particular $E_iT_{i,c,t}\in U_A^0E_i$, $F_iT_{i,c,t}\in U_A^0F_i$,
$T_{i,c,t}E_i=E_iT_{i,c+2,t}\in E_iU_A^0$ and
$T_{i,c,t}F_i=F_iT_{i,c-2,t}\in F_iU_A^0$: the toral factor can be moved to the
middle at the cost of a shift of the binomial index.

(iii) **Reordering identity.** For all $a,b\ge0$,
$$E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(b)}=\sum_{t=0}^{\min(a,b)}F_i^{(b-t)}\,T_{i,\,2t-a-b,\,t}\,E_i^{(a-t)},$$
with every coefficient a toral quantum binomial in $U_A^0$. In particular
$E_iF_i-F_iE_i=T_{i,0,1}$ and
$E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(a)}=\sum_{t=0}^{a}F_i^{(a-t)}T_{i,2t-2a,t}E_i^{(a-t)}$.
For $i\ne j$, $E_i^{(a)}$ and $F_j^{(b)}$ commute; the same-half divided powers
$E_i^{(a)},E_j^{(b)}$ (and likewise $F_i^{(a)},F_j^{(b)}$) commute whenever
$a_{ij}=0$, and for $a_{ij}\ne0$ no commutation is asserted.

(iv) **Triangular spanning.** Every element of $U_A$ is an $A$-linear
combination of products $b_-u\,b_+$ with $b_-\in U_A^-$, $u\in U_A^0$ and
$b_+\in U_A^+$; equivalently $U_A=U_A^-U_A^0U_A^+$ as an $A$-module. No
independence of the spanning family is asserted.

Let $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra of a finite symmetrizable Cartan datum, over $k=\mathbb Q(q)$, and let $U_q^-,U_q^0,U_q^+$ be its generated subalgebras of [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]].

(i) Multiplication is a vector-space isomorphism
$$m:U_q^-\otimes_k U_q^0\otimes_k U_q^+\longrightarrow U_q(\mathfrak g),\qquad x_-\otimes x_0\otimes x_+\longmapsto x_-x_0x_+.$$
Products $b_-K_h b_+$, with $b_\pm$ ranging over supplied bases of the two halves and $h\in P^\vee$, form a basis of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$. Arbitrary simple-generator words span the halves; their Serre relations preclude claiming their independence.

(ii) The halves are exactly the algebras presented by their separate Serre relations, and $U_q^0\cong k[P^\vee]$. Thus all three abstract factor maps are injective and the $K_h$ are linearly independent.

(iii) For every $\beta\in Q$, the total root grading satisfies
$$U_q(\mathfrak g)[\beta]\cong\bigoplus_{\alpha,\gamma\in Q_+,\,\alpha-\gamma=\beta} U_q^-[-\gamma]\otimes_k U_q^0\otimes_k U_q^+[\alpha].$$
In particular degree zero contains all equal-positive/negative-degree summands, including $F_iE_i$; it is not just the toral subalgebra. As a left $U_q^0$-module this component is free, with rank equal to the possibly infinite sum of the products of the two half-component dimensions. Under AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the half-component dimensions are their classical PBW ranks, and products of the generic PBW bases of [[thm-generic-quantum-serre-halves-have-classical-pbw-ranks-and-a-nondegenerate-hopf-pairing]] with the toral basis give a PBW basis of the whole algebra. AC enters only through that supplier's formal-embedding proof; (i), (ii) and the graded tensor decomposition are choice-free.

For any finite sequence of based integrable modules in the finite-weight-space category $O_{\mathrm{int}}$, the field tensor bar $\Psi=\Theta(\text{composite factor bars})$, built from the normalized intertwiner $\Theta$ of [[thm-the-weightwise-quasi-r-intertwiner-exists-and-is-unique]], is well defined, semilinear, $U$- and bar-compatible, involutive and independent of all parenthesizations; all root-height sums are vectorwise finite.

For arbitrary four-axiom based integrable factors in finite Cartan type, the same field assertion and integral lattice preservation hold without multiplicity or global weight bounds, by the finite-action and universal integral-coefficient clauses of [[lem-quasi-r-divided-power-integrality-on-based-lattices]]. Their actual bar is weight-transfer triangular with diagonal $1$. Finite action and integrality do not imply finite supported normalized global lifts: the periodic rank-one construction of [[lem-periodic-cyclotomic-based-sl-two-tensor-corrections-escape-every-finite-cut]] refutes that additional unrestricted assertion and the natural integral balanced tensor triple.

The full based and globalization assertion holds for bounded $O_{\mathrm{int}}$ pairs with independently established integral action (in particular for finite Cartan type), and for the supported construction cases of the supplier: highest-first or first $C_{\mathrm{high}}$ with arbitrary based second; arbitrary based first with lowest or $C_{\mathrm{low}}$ second; finite highest products and exact based subquotients and weight-admissible direct sums of their tensor constructions; and ordered highest-prefix, based-middle, lowest-suffix products with their explicit support bounds. This includes the full finite-dimensional tensor product, with every constituent, in finite Cartan type. For any further class, the globalization assertion requires independently proved integral action and finite raw-basis correction closure in the strict weight-transfer order.

In these supported cases the actual tensor global vectors are uniquely corrected bar-fixed lifts of the raw tensor residue vectors, with corrections in $q\mathbb Z[q]$; the transition and its inverse have finite columns, the corrected vectors form an $A$-basis, and the integral tensor triple is balanced. The $q=0$ tensor crystal lattice is supplied separately by [[thm-crystal-basis-tensor-product-rule]], and its actual infinity chart is $\Psi(L_0^{\mathrm{tensor}})$. Exact based integral bar-compatible subquotient maps preserve corrected global bases by balanced uniqueness, within these supported constructions. Raw tensor lower vectors need not be bar fixed. The affine boundary of the integral-action supplier still disproves arbitrary based-pair integral action in general type. No universal-$R$ braiding or uncontrolled semi-infinite evaluation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the integral global-basis suppliers. Let $(M,B)$ be a finite dimensional integrable based module of finite Cartan type in the exact four-axiom sense of [[def-the-bar-lattice-and-integral-lattice-of-a-based-module]], and let $M_A=\bigoplus_{b\in B}Ab$. There is a finite filtration of $M_A$ by $U_A$-stable submodules, each spanned by a subset of its actual basis, with successive quotients isomorphic to integral highest lattices $V_A(\lambda)$. Every quotient is finite free. Specializing at any nonzero complex parameter therefore gives an actual Weyl filtration, with all injections retained. This is an integral filtration statement, not a generic decomposition assertion.

Under [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$ is a nonzero finite dimensional integrable type-1 module, cyclic on a highest vector of label $\lambda$ with one-dimensional highest space. Its formal character is the classical finite Weyl character $\chi_\lambda$. It is universal among finite dimensional highest-label modules generated by a vector of label $\lambda$. It has a unique maximal proper submodule and unique simple head $L_\zeta(\lambda)$. The simple heads are pairwise nonisomorphic and exhaust finite dimensional simple type-1 modules. The dual Weyl module has the same character, unique simple socle $L_\zeta(\lambda)$, and weights at most $\lambda$.

These assertions use the inherited Axiom of Choice. They do not assert root-specialized semisimplicity or that these Weyl modules are simple.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For the actual root Weyl families of [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], Weyl-filtered and dual-Weyl-filtered modules are closed under direct summands. Hence tiltings are closed under direct summands, and each tilting is a finite direct sum of indecomposable tiltings. One has $\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_\zeta(\lambda),\nabla_\zeta(\mu))=\delta_{\lambda\mu}\mathbb C$ and every extension of a Weyl-filtered module by a dual-Weyl-filtered module splits. Every indecomposable tilting has a unique maximal label, of multiplicity one, and two indecomposable tiltings with the same maximal label are isomorphic. These assertions give uniqueness where the objects exist; they make no existence claim for an arbitrary prescribed label.

derivations.claim: We first prove the integral cyclic presentation used below. For dominant $a,b$ put $\xi=b-a$ and let $C_A(\xi)$ be the universal cyclic $U_A$-module on a vector with full toral character $\xi$, without a highest or lowest annihilation requirement. Mixed reordering makes its ordered positive-negative half products span. Their independence follows by applying them to the tensor of a lowest Verma vector of label $-a$ and a highest Verma vector of label $b$: in the two Verma half lattices the leading action of an ordered positive-negative product is the corresponding pure tensor, with a Laurent unit as coefficient, and all other terms have smaller half degree. Induction on the sum of the two nonnegative root heights in this unit triangular transformation gives an integral isomorphism of $C_A(\xi)$ with this tensor of the two free Verma lattices. Thus no torsionfreeness-to-freeness or generic direct-sum inference enters.

Quotient the two Verma half lattices by their actual integrable highest or lowest kernels from [F1]. Under the map in step 1.1 the kernel from the highest factor is exactly $\sum_i\sum_{r>b(h_i)}U_AF_i^{(r)}v_\xi$, and the kernel from the lowest factor is exactly $\sum_i\sum_{r>a(h_i)}U_AE_i^{(r)}v_\xi$. To check these equalities, use the positive-negative ordered products for the first assertion and the negative-positive ordered products for the second: the rightmost divided power acts on the relevant highest or lowest generator, while the other extreme generator is killed by that color's opposite action. The leading term is the corresponding singular half vector and the correction terms have smaller half degrees; degree induction gives both inclusions. The half kernels are the sums of the specified divided-power ideals by [F1], so summing gives the whole tensor kernel. Consequently $\omega V_A(a)\otimes_A V_A(b)$ is the cyclic module on $v_\xi$ with exactly these two families of annihilation relations. Here $\omega$ interchanges positive and negative generators and negates weight labels. Both tensor factors are finite free, so specialization preserves this exact presentation by right exactness. This is the integral lowest-highest presentation, not a claim about an arbitrary integral lattice.

Put $\Pi=\bigcup_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\operatorname{Wt}\Delta_\zeta(\gamma)$, with formal label weights rather than torus eigenvalues. It is finite. A finite module has composition labels in $\Gamma$ exactly when all its weights lie in $\Pi$: one direction follows from character additivity, and conversely each simple factor's dominant highest label $\mu$ belongs to $\Pi$, hence is at most some $\gamma\in\Gamma$, so saturation puts $\mu$ in $\Gamma$. For a fixed $\xi\in\Pi$, choose $a,b\in P^+$ with $b-a=\xi$ and with every $a(h_i),b(h_i)$ larger than the maximum possible length of any $i$-string starting at any label in $\Pi$. Such $a$ exists by taking an integral multiple of $\rho$ sufficiently large, then setting $b=a+\xi$. Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited through the integral-basis and finite-type quasi-$R$ coefficient suppliers. In the exact simply connected, simply-laced, full-weight-lattice and odd $\ell>h$ branch of [[def-full-toral-weight-root-of-unity-module-category]], the category $\mathcal C_\zeta$ is a $\mathbb C$-linear abelian braided rigid monoidal category. The tensor action is the specialized full divided-power coproduct, the unit is the counit module, and finite left and right duals use $S$ and $S^{-1}$, respectively. On the left double dual its pivotal structure is

$$j_M(v)(f)=f(gv),\qquad g=K_{-2\rho^\vee},\qquad 2\rho^\vee=\sum_{\alpha>0}\alpha^\vee.$$

The two pivotal traces are $\operatorname{Tr}_M(gf)$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_M(g^{-1}f)$, and they are equal for every endomorphism $f$. Thus the pivotal structure is spherical in the strong trace sense.

Here is an actual compatible braiding, for the bicharacter $\chi$ fixed in the definition. Let $\Theta_\zeta$ be the specialization of the integral finite-type quasi-$R$ coefficients in the positive-first/negative-second convention of [[thm-the-weightwise-quasi-r-intertwiner-exists-and-is-unique]]. Let $D_{M,N}$ act on $M_\lambda\otimes N_\mu$ by $\chi(\lambda,\mu)$ and set

$$R_{M,N}=D_{M,N}^{-1}(\Theta^{-1})_{M,N},\qquad c_{M,N}=\tau\circ R_{M,N}.$$

Every series here acts as a finite sum; $R$ intertwines the full specialized algebra, including every higher divided power and every toral binomial, and satisfies both coproduct identities giving the two hexagons. No determinant coprimality restriction is needed for this braided structure; no nondegeneracy or modularity is asserted.

Under [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], and the inherited Axiom of Choice, the tensor product of two Weyl-filtered modules is Weyl-filtered, and the tensor product of two dual-Weyl-filtered modules is dual-Weyl-filtered. Hence tilting modules are closed under tensor products, ordinary duals and finite direct sums, and contain the tensor unit. This theorem does not presume direct-summand closure or classify indecomposable tiltings.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For the actual root Weyl families of [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], Weyl-filtered and dual-Weyl-filtered modules are closed under direct summands. Hence tiltings are closed under direct summands, and each tilting is a finite direct sum of indecomposable tiltings. One has $\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_\zeta(\lambda),\nabla_\zeta(\mu))=\delta_{\lambda\mu}\mathbb C$ and every extension of a Weyl-filtered module by a dual-Weyl-filtered module splits. Every indecomposable tilting has a unique maximal label, of multiplicity one, and two indecomposable tiltings with the same maximal label are isomorphic. These assertions give uniqueness where the objects exist; they make no existence claim for an arbitrary prescribed label.

Fix a rigid monoidal category with chosen left duals. For a morphism
$a:X\to X^{\vee\vee}$, the **left categorical trace** of $a$ is the endomorphism
of the unit

$$\operatorname{Tr}_L(a):\mathbf 1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{coev}_X}X\otimes X^\vee\xrightarrow{a\otimes1_{X^\vee}}X^{\vee\vee}\otimes X^\vee\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_{X^\vee}}\mathbf 1.$$

For a morphism $b:X^{\vee\vee}\to X$, the **right categorical trace** of $b$ is

$$\operatorname{Tr}_R(b):\mathbf 1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{coev}_{X^\vee}}X^\vee\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{1_{X^\vee}\otimes b}X^\vee\otimes X\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_X}\mathbf 1.$$

So a bare endomorphism $X\to X$ is not yet an input to categorical trace; one
first needs a comparison between $X$ and a double dual.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For $f:X\to Y$ and $b:Y\to X$, rectangular matrix multiplication gives $\operatorname{Tr}_X(g_Xbf)=\operatorname{Tr}_Y(fg_Xb)=\operatorname{Tr}_Y(g_Yfb)$, because module morphisms commute with $g$. In bases, the rectangular trace identity is simply equality of the two finite sums $\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ji}=\sum_{j,i}B_{ji}A_{ij}$. Thus $t_X(bf)=t_Y(fb)$. Linearity makes each $\mathcal N(X,Y)$ a vector subspace. If $f$ is negligible, $a:W\to X$, $c:Y\to Z$, and $d:Z\to W$, cyclicity rewrites $t_W(dcfa)$ as $t_X(adcf)=0$, since $adc:Y\to X$ is a valid test morphism. Hence negligible morphisms form a composition ideal.

By [F3] every tilting is a finite direct sum of indecomposable tiltings. For an indecomposable $T$, generalized eigenspaces of a module endomorphism $a$ are stable graded submodules, and their polynomial spectral projections are module maps. Indecomposability therefore forces one eigenvalue $\lambda$, so $a=\lambda1_T+n$ with $n$ nilpotent. The operator $n$ commutes with $g$, whence $(gn)^r=g^rn^r=0$ for large $r$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(gn)=0$. Consequently $t_T(a)=\lambda d_T$, where $d_T=\operatorname{Tr}_T(g)$. The nonunits of $\operatorname{End}(T)$ are exactly its nilpotents. Each nonunit $n$ lies in the Jacobson radical: for any $a$, the product $an$ cannot be invertible as a finite-dimensional linear map, so it is nilpotent too, making $1-an$ invertible by a finite geometric sum. Conversely a unit cannot lie in the radical. The radical quotient is $\mathbb C$, because $a-\lambda1_T$ is a nonunit and every scalar class is represented. If $d_T=0$, every endomorphism has zero trace and $1_T$ is negligible. If $d_T\ne0$, testing against the identity and using the radical ideal property shows $a$ is negligible exactly when $a$ is in that radical. Thus every retained indecomposable has scalar endomorphism ring in the quotient.

In a basis $z_i$ and its dual $z_i^*$ it is $k(y)=\sum_i(1_X\otimes z_i^*)(1_X\otimes g_Z)b(y\otimes z_i)$. Tensoring $f$ with an arbitrary morphism is a further composition with an identity tensor that morphism, hence is negligible too. This proves the two-sided tensor-ideal assertion without assuming that endomorphisms of a tensor product factor into tensor products.

If indecomposables $T,U$ are not isomorphic and $f:T\to U$, then $bf$ is not invertible for every $b:U\to T$. Otherwise $f$ and $(bf)^{-1}b$ split $T$ as a nonzero direct summand of $U$, and indecomposability would force an isomorphism. Therefore $bf$ is nilpotent by step 1.2, and $t_T(bf)=0$. All morphisms between nonisomorphic indecomposables are negligible. For isomorphic summands, transport by an isomorphism and use the radical description of step 1.2. On finite direct sums the trace is the sum of the diagonal block traces. Testing a single opposite block makes negligibility entrywise in any indecomposable decomposition. Hence quotient morphisms are precisely finite block matrices over $\mathbb C$ on the multiplicity spaces of the retained isomorphism classes, with no morphisms between different classes. This proves semisimplicity, and every matrix idempotent splits by ordinary finite-dimensional linear algebra within sums of the retained objects, proving idempotent completeness.

The ideal proved in steps 1.1–2.1 permits composition and tensor product to descend to the quotient. The evaluations, coevaluations, associators, unit maps, braiding and pivotal maps descend; their identities remain true because a quotient preserves equations and identities. Their traces are the images of the original scalar traces, so the strong spherical equality of [F1] descends as well. The unit is retained since $d_{\mathbf1}=1$; its one-dimensional underlying space has scalar endomorphisms and is indecomposable, so it is simple in the quotient. The Hom spaces are finite dimensional by [F1]. If there are finitely many retained classes, these facts give exactly a fusion category. All finiteness and label identifications beyond this condition are excluded from the conclusion and must be supplied by their actual subsequent proofs. The zero tilting becomes zero, and all constructions above use finite decompositions and sums; inherited Choice is confined to [F5].

There is $b\equiv a\pmod l$ with $\gcd(b,ld)=1$: for every prime dividing $d$ but not $l$ avoid the unique forbidden residue of the multiplier in $b=a+kl$, and apply the finite Chinese remainder theorem; primes dividing $l$ already do not divide $b$. Thus $t=\exp(2\pi i b/(ld))$ is a primitive $ld$-th root with $t^d=\zeta$. Use [F3] with this auxiliary root. Replacing a previously selected $d$-th root by this one does not change the underlying module category or pivot; the ratio of the two Cartan phases is trivial whenever one label belongs to $Q$, hence is a bicharacter of $P/Q$. We use this auxiliary braiding only to construct natural module endomorphisms, with no nondegeneracy claim for either braiding.

For every Weyl module $V=\Delta_\zeta(\nu)$ define $z_V(M)$ as the pivotal partial trace over $V$ of the monodromy $R_{21}R$ on $M\otimes V$. This is an $H$-linear natural endomorphism of $M$ by [F3]. On a highest vector $v_\lambda$ of $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$ the first $R$ has only its Cartan term, since every positive first-factor correction kills $v_\lambda$. In the second $R_{21}$ each nonzero root-degree term raises the $V$ label; its pivotal trace is zero because the pivot preserves labels. The scalar on the highest line is therefore $c_\nu(\lambda)=\sum_{\eta\in P}\dim(V_\eta)\,\chi(-2(\lambda+\rho),\eta).$ Here the two Cartan terms contribute $\chi(\lambda,\eta)^{-2}$ and the pivot contributes $\zeta^{-(2\rho,\eta)}=\chi(-2\rho,\eta)$, since $2\rho\in Q$. Because the Weyl module is cyclic and $z_V$ is a module map, it is this scalar on the whole module. Its value on the simple head is the same.

Put $K=\{x\in P:\chi(2x,\eta)=1\text{ for all }\eta\in P\}$. It has finite index in $P$ because it contains $lQ$. The characters of $G$ obtained from the second argument therefore give all characters of $G$, because the induced injection from $G$ into its character group is between finite groups of equal order. Their independence follows directly by summing each character over $G$: a nontrivial character sum is zero by translation by a point where it is nontrivial, and the trivial character sum is $|G|$.

Classical Weyl characters span the $W$-invariant group algebra $\mathbb C[P]^W$. Indeed $\chi_
u$ has leading orbit sum at dominant weight $
u$ with coefficient one and only strictly smaller dominant orbit labels below it; induction on the finite downward set eliminates these smaller terms and writes every orbit sum as a finite linear combination of Weyl characters. Evaluation on $G$ maps these orbit sums to the averages under $W$ of the character basis from step 2.2. Those averages span all $W$-invariant functions on $G$, since averaging commutes with Fourier expansion. In particular they distinguish different $W$-orbits of $G$ by the characteristic functions of those orbits. Thus equality $c_
u(\lambda)=c_
u(\mu)$ for every dominant $
u$ forces $\mu+ho=w(\lambda+ho)+k$ for some $w\in W$ and $k\in K$. This finite Fourier argument requires neither an invertible modular $S$-matrix nor simplicity of root Weyl modules.

If a simple $L_\zeta(\mu)$ is a composition factor of $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$, these projections force $\mu-\lambda\in Q$, and every $z_V$ acts on that factor by the scalar on the original Weyl module. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 therefore give $k\in K\cap Q$. For $l=2\ell$ this intersection is $\ell Q$. For $l=\ell$ odd, writing $k=(\ell/2)\sum n_i\alpha_i\in Q$ forces every $n_i$ even by the simple-root basis and oddness of $\ell$, so again $K\cap Q=\ell Q$. Consequently $\mu$ and $\lambda$ lie in the same $W\ltimes\ell Q$ dot orbit. Their dominance inequality follows from the support of the Weyl module in [F1].

All the endomorphisms $z_V(M)$ commute: naturality of $z_V$ with respect to the module endomorphism $z_{V'}(M)$ gives commutation. On a fixed finite dimensional $M$, their span in $\operatorname{End}(M)$ is finite dimensional, so finitely many suffice to determine all their joint generalized eigenspaces. If $M$ is indecomposable tilting, it has only one such block and only one $P/Q$ coset. Every Weyl section therefore has the same scalar tuple as the section of its highest label $\lambda$, and step 4.1 places every section label in the same affine orbit. The standard-costandard degree-one vanishing in [F2] extends to all positive degrees. For $j\ge2$, the projective sequence for $\Delta_\eta$ in [F1] identifies $\operatorname{Ext}^j(\Delta_\eta,
abla_\mu)$ with $\operatorname{Ext}^{j-1}(K_\eta,
abla_\mu)$; a Weyl flag of $K_\eta$ and induction on $j$ make the latter zero. Filtering either variable proves all positive Ext groups vanish between any Weyl-filtered and dual-Weyl-filtered pair. Likewise, if $N$ satisfies $\operatorname{Ext}^1(N,
abla_\mu)=0$ for every label, then the injective sequences in [F1] give all positive groups zero: filter their dual-Weyl cokernels and dimension shift successively in the second variable. In particular Ext from $N$ in every positive degree vanishes against any dual-Weyl-filtered module.

Let $\eta$ be maximal in $\Gamma$ and $e$ its primitive idempotent. Then $Ae=P_\eta=\Delta_\eta$ and $eAe=\mathbb C$. Apply the canonical maximal-Weyl-trace argument of [F2] to each projective column and sum the columns: multiplication gives an injection $Ae\otimes_\mathbb C eA\to A$ with image $J=AeA$. Thus $J$ is projective on both sides. The quotient $A'=A/J$ models the Serre subcategory on $\Gamma\setminus\{\eta\}$. Its projective columns are obtained by removing the maximal trace from the old projectives, so they retain the other Weyl sections; equivalently this is exactly the smaller root truncation in [F1]. Its injectives are dual-Weyl-filtered, with unchanged smaller-label families.

Suppose $N$ has the Ext vanishing of step 1.1. Choose a projective resolution $P_\bullet\to N$ with finite dimensional projective terms, and tensor it with $A'$. Each resulting term is projective over $A'$. For any injective $A'$-module $I'$, adjunction identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_{A'}(A'\otimes_A P_\bullet,I')$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_A(P_\bullet,I')$, whose positive cohomology is zero by step 1.1 and the dual Weyl filtration of $I'$. Exactness of Hom into an injective identifies that cohomology with Hom from the corresponding homology module. Injectives detect nonzero homology: a nonzero finite homology module has a simple submodule $L$; embed $L$ into its injective envelope $I_L$ and extend that map to the homology module by injectivity. The extension is nonzero on $L$, so Hom into $I_L$ is nonzero. No assertion that one copy of each injective envelope embeds every finite module is needed. Hence $\operatorname{Tor}^A_j(A',N)=0$ for all $j>0$. Tensoring $0\to J\to A\to A'\to0$ therefore gives the actual exact sequence $0\to Ae\otimes_\mathbb C eN\to N\to N'\to0$, $N'=A'\otimes_A N$.

The exact tensor resolution from step 2.1 and adjunction give $\operatorname{Ext}^j_{A'}(N',\nabla_\mu)=\operatorname{Ext}^j_A(N,\nabla_\mu)=0$ for every smaller label and every $j>0$. Induct on $|\Gamma|$ to conclude $N'$ is Weyl-filtered; the base empty category contains only zero. The kernel in step 2.1 is a direct sum of $\Delta_\eta$, so $N$ is Weyl-filtered. The converse is step 1.1. Exact ordinary duality in the relabelled finite truncation $\Gamma^*=-w_0\Gamma$ proves the asserted dual-Weyl criterion. This proves the needed Ext criteria rather than importing them from category $\mathcal O$.

Fix $\lambda$ and take the finite saturated ideal $\Gamma=\{\mu\in P^+:\mu\le\lambda\}$. Start with $X=\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$ and process the other labels in a linear order descending in dominance. At the step for $\mu$, let $m=\dim\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta_\mu,X)$ and choose the universal extension $0\to X\to X'\to\Delta_\mu^{\oplus m}\to0$ whose components are a basis of that Ext space. The connecting map from $\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_\mu,\Delta_\mu^{\oplus m})$ onto this Ext space is an isomorphism because $\operatorname{End}(\Delta_\mu)=\mathbb C$. Also $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta_\mu,\Delta_\mu)=0$ by the highest-vector splitting lemma, so the exact sequence of Ext makes $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta_\mu,X')=0$. Already processed labels $\nu$ stay killed: they are not strictly below $\mu$, and the same splitting lemma gives $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta_\nu,\Delta_\mu)=0$. The original top label is killed from the start. Every step preserves a Weyl flag, top multiplicity one and support at most $\lambda$. Finite dimensionality of the algebra in [F1] makes each Ext space finite dimensional and the process finite.

The final $X$ has all the degree-one vanishings in the costandard criterion of step 3.1, so it is dual-Weyl-filtered as well as Weyl-filtered, hence tilting. Decompose it into indecomposable tiltings using [F2]. Exactly one summand contains its one-dimensional $\lambda$ space. That summand has highest label $\lambda$, multiplicity one, and normalized bottom inclusion by the maximal trace lemma; all remaining Weyl labels are strictly smaller. Call it $T_\zeta(\lambda)$. Its uniqueness and the decomposition of every tilting into the objects so obtained follow from [F2]. All constructions occur in an actual finite root truncation, so these are genuine module filtrations and objects in the full category.
