Use the affine-wall notation and componentwise fundamental alcove $A$ from [[def-cg-affine-root-hyperplane-reflection-and-alcove]] and [[lem-cg-highest-root-and-fundamental-alcove]]. Let $J$ be the affine facet-type set from [[lem-cg-affine-alcove-separation-and-facet-types]], with one label $0_i$ for each nonempty irreducible component, and let $s_a$ be the reflection in the fundamental facet of type $a\in J$. Let $W_{\rm abs}$, its Coxeter matrix $m_{ab}=\operatorname{ord}(s_as_b)$, and $\varphi:W_{\rm abs}\to W_a$ be those of [[lem-cg-affine-generic-gallery-paths-and-disk-moves]]; its finite labels are $2,3,4,6$, and $m_{ab}=\infty$ only for the two opposite facets of a rank-one component. If $J=\varnothing$, take $W_{\rm abs}=W_a=\{1\}$.

**(1) Transitivity and generation.** The subgroup $G:=\langle s_a:a\in J\rangle\le W_a$ equals $W_a$, and $W_a$ acts transitively on the set of alcoves. Every affine wall supports a facet of the closure of some alcove; if $H$ is a facet wall of $g(A)$, its reflection is $g s_a g^{-1}$ for the type $a$ of that facet.

**(2) Presentation and simple transitivity.** The homomorphism $\varphi:W_{\rm abs}\to W_a$ is an isomorphism. Thus $W_a$ is the Coxeter group with simple system $(s_a)_{a\in J}$, and it acts simply transitively on alcoves: for any two alcoves $C,C'$ there is exactly one $g\in W_a$ such that $g(C)=C'$.

**(3) Length.** Let $\ell(g)$ be the minimum number of facet reflections from $(s_a)_{a\in J}$ whose product is $g$. For every $g\in W_a$,
$$\ell(g)=\#\operatorname{Sep}(A,g(A)),$$
where $\operatorname{Sep}$ is the separating-wall set of [[lem-cg-affine-alcove-separation-and-facet-types]]. A straight generic segment between interior points of $A$ and $g(A)$ crosses each separating wall exactly once and gives a gallery attaining the minimum. The argument includes rank-one factors and reducible systems with the product conventions of [[lem-cg-highest-root-and-fundamental-alcove]] (3).

**(4) Comparison.** The finite root-system types are the standard crystallographic types $A_n,B_n,C_n,D_n,E_6,E_7,E_8,F_4,G_2$ (with the low-rank identifications in [[thm-classification-of-irreducible-reduced-crystallographic-root-systems]]). In that root-system normalization, $W_a=Q^\vee\rtimes W$ from [[lem-cg-affine-reflection-identities-and-local-finiteness]] is the standard affine Weyl group. This does not identify it with an untwisted Kac–Moody loop realization, and it does not assert that the extended group $P^\vee\rtimes W$ is a Coxeter group with the same simple system. No axiom of choice is used.

Under [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$ is a nonzero finite dimensional integrable type-1 module, cyclic on a highest vector of label $\lambda$ with one-dimensional highest space. Its formal character is the classical finite Weyl character $\chi_\lambda$. It is universal among finite dimensional highest-label modules generated by a vector of label $\lambda$. It has a unique maximal proper submodule and unique simple head $L_\zeta(\lambda)$. The simple heads are pairwise nonisomorphic and exhaust finite dimensional simple type-1 modules. The dual Weyl module has the same character, unique simple socle $L_\zeta(\lambda)$, and weights at most $\lambda$.

These assertions use the inherited Axiom of Choice. They do not assert root-specialized semisimplicity or that these Weyl modules are simple.

Use the full simply-laced weight lattice $P$, root lattice $Q$, parameter $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta^2)=\ell$ odd greater than $h$, and full type-1 category of [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]]. If $L_\zeta(\mu)$ is a composition factor of $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$, then $\mu\le\lambda$ and $\mu\in(W\ltimes\ell Q)\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda$. More generally every Weyl section and every composition factor of an indecomposable tilting module of highest label $\lambda$ has label in this same affine orbit. These claims hold for both possible orders $\ell$ and $2\ell$ of $\zeta$, with no coprimality condition on the index $[P:Q]$. They use the inherited Axiom of Choice.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Choice. For each dominant weight $\lambda$ there exists a unique indecomposable tilting module $T_\zeta(\lambda)$ with highest label $\lambda$. It has a normalized inclusion $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)\hookrightarrow T_\zeta(\lambda)$ with Weyl-filtered cokernel of strictly smaller labels and highest multiplicity one. Every tilting module is a finite direct sum of these. In every finite saturated truncation $\mathcal C_\Gamma$ one has
$$
M\text{ is dual-Weyl-filtered}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta_\zeta(\mu),M)=0\text{ for all }\mu\in\Gamma,
$$
and the dual Weyl-filtration criterion with the variables interchanged. No semisimplicity or alcove dimension assertion is included here.

Use [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], normalize every root to have squared length two, and use the pivot $g=K_{-2\rho^\vee}$ from [[thm-root-of-unity-lusztig-module-category-is-braided-rigid]]. With the inherited Axiom of Choice,
$$
\operatorname{qdim}\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)=\prod_{\alpha>0}\frac{[\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle]_\zeta}{[\langle\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle]_\zeta}.
$$
Every denominator is nonzero. Extend the displayed product to all integral $\lambda$. It is alternating under the dot action of $W$ and periodic under translation by $\ell Q$, hence satisfies $d(w\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda)=\det(w)d(\lambda)$ for the affine Weyl group $W_\ell=W\ltimes\ell Q$. Its zero set is exactly the affine singular weights. In particular all weights in the open bottom alcove have nonzero Weyl quantum dimension. Every Weyl-filtered module all of whose section labels are affine singular has quantum dimension zero. No assertion about arbitrary outside-alcove indecomposable tiltings is inferred without a proof about their actual section labels or their tensor-ideal generation.

derivations.claim: Define the folding map $p$ on an open alcove $wC^\circ$ by $p(x)=w^{-1}x$. It extends continuously across facets: the two inverse maps on adjacent alcoves differ by the corresponding fundamental-facet reflection, which fixes their common facet pointwise. At a point on several walls, use a small ball meeting only the finitely many incident walls; its local chambers are connected by adjacent local chambers, so the same agreement proves that all limiting inverse maps coincide there. This yields a continuous map on the whole Euclidean space, identity on $C$, and $p(wx)=p(x)$ for every affine Weyl element. On a line segment crossing walls generically, local finiteness divides it into finitely many pieces on each of which $p$ is an isometry, so the distance of the images of its endpoints is at most its length. General endpoints follow by arbitrarily small perturbation of the endpoints to avoid the finitely many codimension-two wall intersections and passage to continuity. Hence $p$ is one-Lipschitz.

The origin belongs to $C$, so $p(0)=0$. Thus for $x\in C$ and any affine Weyl element $w$, step 1.1 gives $\|x\|=\|p(wx)-p(0)\|\le\|wx\|$. Put $x=\lambda+\rho$. If a dominant $\mu<\lambda$ belonged to its dot orbit, then $\mu+\rho=wx$ while $\|\lambda+\rho\|^2-\|\mu+\rho\|^2=(\lambda-\mu,\lambda+\mu+2\rho)>0$: expand the nonzero positive-root-lattice vector $\lambda-\mu$ in simple roots and use strict positivity of every pairing with $\lambda+\mu+2\rho$. This contradicts the norm inequality. By [F2] there is no proper composition factor of $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$, and it is simple.

The dual Weyl module has a unique simple socle at the same label and the same character and dimension, so it too equals that simple module. This object is consequently tilting, and uniqueness identifies it with $T_\zeta(\lambda)$. By [F3] its quantum dimension is nonzero in the strict bottom alcove and zero on the upper wall, proving all assertions.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Choice. Use the simply-laced full-weight datum and root parameter of [[def-full-toral-weight-root-of-unity-module-category]], with $\ell=\operatorname{ord}(\zeta^2)$ odd and $\ell>h$. Write $L=\operatorname{ord}(\zeta)$, so $L=\ell$ or $2\ell$. In the toral quotient $\overline U=U^L_\zeta/(K_i^L-1:i\in I)$ let $u$ be the ordinary-generator image generated by all $E_i,F_i,K_i^{\pm1}$. This quotient acts on every full type-1 module; it is not an assertion that $K_i^\ell=1$ in the unmodified algebra.

For every reduced convex root ordering, $u^\pm$ have the ordinary root monomial bases with every exponent in $\{0,\ldots,\ell-1\}$, and multiplication gives $u^-\otimes\mathbb C[(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^I]\otimes u^+\cong u$. Thus $\dim u=L^{|I|}\ell^{2|\Phi^+|}$. The braid symmetries specialize to automorphisms of $u$ and transport these triangular decompositions to every transformed Borel. For $p_i=\langle u^0,u^+,F_i\rangle$, $u$ is free on both sides over $p_i$; complementary negative-root monomials are right-module basis elements when the negative convex ordering ends in $\alpha_i$. The same freeness holds after braid transport. All these assertions retain the formal $P$-grading on modules.

The ordinary negative Borel $u^-u^0$ is a finite Hopf algebra; no claim is made that a general braid-transformed Borel is a Hopf subalgebra.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional Hopf algebra over a field $k$. For every nonzero left integral functional $\lambda\in\int_{H^*}^{\ell}$, the map
$$
\Phi:H\to H^*,\qquad \Phi(a)(b)=\lambda(ab)
$$
is an isomorphism. Consequently $(a,b)\mapsto\lambda(ab)$ is an associative nondegenerate bilinear form and $H$ is a Frobenius algebra. More explicitly, for every basis $(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ of $H$ there is a unique basis $(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ satisfying $\lambda(u_jv_i)=\delta_{ji}$, and
$$
a=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda(av_i)u_i=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda(u_i a)v_i\qquad(a\in H).
$$

Assume the inherited Axiom of Choice. For every finite saturated subset $\Gamma\subset P^+$ (meaning $\lambda\in\Gamma$, $\mu\in P^+$ and $\mu\le\lambda$ imply $\mu\in\Gamma$), the full root module subcategory $\mathcal C_\Gamma$ with composition labels in $\Gamma$ is equivalent to the category of finite dimensional modules over a finite dimensional complex algebra. It has projective covers $P_\lambda$ and injective envelopes $I_\lambda$ and exact sequences
$$
0\longrightarrow K_\lambda\longrightarrow P_\lambda\longrightarrow\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)\longrightarrow0,\qquad 0\longrightarrow\nabla_\zeta(\lambda)\longrightarrow I_\lambda\longrightarrow C_\lambda\longrightarrow0,
$$
where $K_\lambda$ is Weyl-filtered by strictly greater labels and $C_\lambda$ is dual-Weyl-filtered by strictly greater labels. Moreover $(P_\lambda:\Delta_\zeta(\mu))=[\nabla_\zeta(\mu):L_\zeta(\lambda)]$. The assertion is about the actual root category, not a generic semisimple fibre.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For the actual root Weyl families of [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], Weyl-filtered and dual-Weyl-filtered modules are closed under direct summands. Hence tiltings are closed under direct summands, and each tilting is a finite direct sum of indecomposable tiltings. One has $\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_\zeta(\lambda),\nabla_\zeta(\mu))=\delta_{\lambda\mu}\mathbb C$ and every extension of a Weyl-filtered module by a dual-Weyl-filtered module splits. Every indecomposable tilting has a unique maximal label, of multiplicity one, and two indecomposable tiltings with the same maximal label are isomorphic. These assertions give uniqueness where the objects exist; they make no existence claim for an arbitrary prescribed label.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Put $R=u^-$ and $H=R\rtimes\mathbb C[T]$. This is an actual finite Hopf algebra: $\Delta(F_i)=F_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes F_i$, the torus is group-like, and the antipode preserves this Borel. The odd-order type-1 toral quotient is a Hopf quotient because the $K_i^\ell-1$ generate a Hopf ideal. The positive-height ideal $R_+$ is nilpotent, and $J=R_+H=HR_+$ is nilpotent with quotient $\mathbb C[T]$. This quotient is semisimple: its commuting toral operators diagonalize simultaneously, since their finite-order minimal polynomials divide separable polynomials $X^d-1$. A nilpotent ideal annihilates every simple module, and a semisimple quotient has zero radical; hence $J=\operatorname{rad}H$ and $R_+=\operatorname{rad}R$.

In rank one of highest coordinate $m=(\kappa,\alpha)$, take $v_j=F^{(j)}v_0$ for $0\le j<\ell$; in the opposite module of lowest coordinate $m'=m-2(\ell-1)$ take $v'_j=E^{(j)}v'_0$. Their actions are $Fv_j=[j+1]v_{j+1}$, $Ev_j=[m-j+1]v_{j-1}$, $Ev'_j=[j+1]v'_{j+1}$ and $Fv'_j=-[m'+j-1]v'_{j-1}$, with out-of-range vectors zero. The map $v_j\mapsto c_jv'_{\ell-1-j}$, where $c_0=1$ and $c_{j+1}=-[m-\ell-j]c_j/[j+1]$, intertwines these actions. For $E$ compatibility use $[\ell-j]=-s[j]$ and $[a-\ell]=s[a]$, where $s=\zeta^\ell\in\{1,-1\}$; $F$ compatibility is its defining recurrence, and the endpoint and toral relations follow from the displayed actions and weights. All denominators are nonzero. If $1\le n\le\ell$ is congruent to $m+1$ modulo $\ell$, then $c_j\ne0$ exactly for $j<n$. The kernel is zero for $n=\ell$ and otherwise is spanned by $v_n,\ldots,v_{\ell-1}$, generated by the singular vector $F^{(n)}v_0$. It is an image of the baby Verma of label $\kappa-n\alpha$: the $i$-th positive generator kills that vector because $[m-n+1]=0$, and the other simple positive generators commute with $F_i$.

By [F2], choose a Frobenius functional $f$ on $H$. Then $b\mapsto[a\mapsto f(ab)]$ identifies the left regular module $H$ with $H^*$ under $(h\phi)(a)=\phi(ah)$. The socle of $H^*$ is the annihilator of $J$, of dimension $\dim(H/J)=|T|$. On the other hand $\operatorname{soc}_H H=\{h:Jh=0\}=\{h:R_+h=0\}=\operatorname{soc}_R H$, since $J=HR_+$. As a left $R$-module, $H=\bigoplus_{t\in T}RK_t$, so $|T|\dim\operatorname{soc}_R R=|T|$. Thus $R$ has one-dimensional regular socle, spanned by its nonzero maximum-height PBW monomial; every positive-height factor annihilates it. This transports to braid-transformed halves and to $u^+$ by algebra isomorphisms; transformed Borels need not be Hopf subalgebras for the original coproduct.

Free right induction from the minimal parabolic in [F1] transports this exact rank-one kernel calculation. For adjacent Borels $w,ws_i$, $\beta=w\alpha_i$ and $w$-highest label $\kappa$, it gives a homomorphism $Z^w(\kappa)\to Z^{ws_i}(\kappa-(\ell-1)\beta)$. If $1\le n\le\ell$ is congruent to $(\kappa+w\rho,\beta)$ modulo $\ell$, its kernel is zero for $n=\ell$ and otherwise is an image of $Z^w(\kappa-n\beta)$. This is exact induction of an actual module map; it is not deduced from character equality.

Each baby Verma is regular over its transformed negative half. Every nonzero submodule therefore contains its lowest PBW line by step 2.1, and that line generates its simple socle. Also $Z(\kappa)$ has a unique simple head $L_u(\kappa)$: the sum of all submodules missing its one-dimensional highest line still misses that line and is the unique maximal submodule. Every finite graded simple has such a highest label, by taking a maximal label in its finite support. Their formal characters are linearly independent, since a maximal highest label in a finite relation occurs with coefficient one only in its own simple character.

Choose a reduced expression $w_0=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_N}$, write $w_j=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_{j-1}}$ and $\beta_j=w_j\alpha_{i_j}>0$, and put $\kappa(w)=\kappa+(\ell-1)(w\rho-\rho)$. Compose step 2.2 along these successive Borels from $Z(\kappa)$ to $Z^{w_0}(\kappa-2(\ell-1)\rho)$. Every module in this chain has the character of $Z(\kappa)$: the transformed root-product character changes by $e^{(\ell-1)(\rho-w\rho)}$, canceled by its label shift. Each map is nonzero on the unique label-$\kappa$ line. Indeed in its source that line has exponent $\ell-1$ along already inverted roots and zero along not-yet-inverted roots. The current positive root $\beta_j$ is not yet inverted, so its rank-one exponent is zero and its image coefficient is $c_0=1$; the complementary free parabolic basis makes the resulting vector nonzero.

The composite image is generated by its label-$\kappa$ line. In the opposite-Borel target this is the maximum-height line of its regular $u^+$ representation, so step 2.1 makes its $u$-span the simple socle. Thus the composite image is the simple head $L_u(\kappa)$ of its source. Every other composition factor $L_u(\eta)$ of $Z(\kappa)$ consequently occurs in its kernel. The successive-image filtration of the kernel of a finite composite places it among the composition factors of one of the individual kernels. Step 2.2 makes that kernel an image of $Z^{w_j}(\kappa(w_j)-n_j\beta_j)$ with $1\le n_j<\ell$ and $n_j\equiv(\kappa+\rho,\beta_j)\pmod\ell$, because $\kappa(w_j)+w_j\rho-(\kappa+\rho)=\ell(w_j\rho-\rho)$. This transformed baby Verma has the character of $Z(\kappa-n_j\beta_j)$; independence of simple characters in step 3.1 transfers the composition factor to that ordinary baby Verma. Repeat: the nonnegative root height of the current highest label minus $\eta$ strictly decreases, so the procedure terminates. Each change $\kappa\mapsto\kappa-n_j\beta_j$ is a strict downward affine reflection, in the level $k\ell=(\kappa+\rho,\beta_j)-n_j$. Hence every baby-Verma composition label satisfies $\eta\preceq_\ell\kappa$.

Let $p(\beta)$ denote the Kostant partition numbers, defined by $\sum_{\beta\in Q_+}p(\beta)e^{-\beta}=\prod_{\alpha>0}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$. The baby PBW character and the actual Weyl formula in [F3] give $\operatorname{ch}Z(\kappa)=e^\kappa\prod_{\alpha>0}\frac{1-e^{-\ell\alpha}}{1-e^{-\alpha}},\qquad \operatorname{ch}\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)=\sum_{w\in W,\,\beta\in Q_+}\det(w)p(\beta)\operatorname{ch}Z(w\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda-\ell\beta).$ The second identity follows by multiplying the finite Weyl numerator by $\prod_{\alpha>0}(1-e^{-\ell\alpha})^{-1}$. It holds in the completion on $\lambda-Q_+$: $w\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda\le\lambda$, and only finitely many $\beta$ contribute to a fixed label. Simple graded characters are a unitriangular basis in that completion: recursively subtract their highest coefficients by increasing root height; every bounded-height interval has finitely many lattice labels, so the recursion is well defined and unique. In particular the coefficient of a fixed simple character on the right is a finite signed sum, since its contributing highest labels must satisfy $w\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda-\ell\beta\ge\eta$.

If $L_\zeta(\eta)$ is a composition factor of $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$, restriction to $u$ is exact and its highest vector generates a baby-Verma quotient with simple head $L_u(\eta)$. Thus $L_u(\eta)$ has positive multiplicity in the actual restricted Weyl module. The finite signed character coefficient in step 4.2 must therefore have some nonzero baby multiplicity, giving $\eta\preceq_\ell w\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda-\ell\beta$ by step 4.1. This uses virtual characters only to locate a composition factor, not to assert a module filtration.

For every $x$ and positive root $\alpha$, the translation $x\mapsto x-\ell\alpha$ is a downward chain. Write $(x,\alpha)=k\ell+r$, $0\le r<\ell$. If $r>0$, reflect in levels $k\ell$ and $(k-1)\ell$, subtracting respectively $r\alpha$ and $(\ell-r)\alpha$; if $r=0$, reflect directly in level $(k-1)\ell$, subtracting $\ell\alpha$. For dominant $\lambda$, $w\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda\preceq_\ell\lambda$ as well: build a reduced word by adjoining simple reflections on the left. At a length-increasing step $s_i v$, $v^{-1}\alpha_i$ is positive, so $(v(\lambda+\rho),\alpha_i)>0$ and the level-zero reflection is downward. Apply the negative translations to the positive-root summands of $\beta$. Thus step 5.1 proves $\eta\preceq_\ell\lambda$ for Weyl composition factors. The isometry $-w_0$ preserves positive roots and these downward chains; exact duality in [F3] proves the same assertion for $\nabla_\zeta(\lambda)$.

Work in the finite dominance ideal $\Gamma=\{\mu\in P^+:\mu\le\lambda\}$ and put $S=\{\mu\in\Gamma:\mu\preceq_\ell\lambda\}$. Reciprocity in [F4] and step 6.1 show that every Weyl section $\Delta_\zeta(
u)$ of the projective kernel $K_\mu$ has $\mu\prec_\ell
u$. Suppose $X$ has all composition labels in $S$ and $\mu
otin S$. Such a section label $
u$ cannot belong to $S$, since transitivity would give $\mu\preceq_\ell\lambda$. Hence $\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_\zeta(
u),X)=0$: a nonzero image is a highest quotient with simple head $L_\zeta(
u)$, absent from $X$. Induction along the kernel flag gives $\operatorname{Hom}(K_\mu,X)=0$. The projective sequence consequently gives $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta_\zeta(\mu),X)=0$.

The actual finite universal-extension construction in [F4] starts with $X=\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$, whose composition labels lie in $S$ by step 6.1. Step 7.1 shows that it never adds a Weyl quotient with label outside $S$. Adding a section with label in $S$ preserves this composition support by step 6.1 and transitivity. The final tilting and its indecomposable highest-label-$\lambda$ summand therefore have all Weyl labels in $S$, using summand closure in [F4]. Their composition labels also lie in $S$ by the Weyl result already proved. This proves every assertion, for both possible orders of $\zeta$ and without primality of $\ell$; the only scalar zeros used were $[a]=0$ exactly when $\ell\mid a$.

citations.quote:
Under [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$ is a nonzero finite dimensional integrable type-1 module, cyclic on a highest vector of label $\lambda$ with one-dimensional highest space. Its formal character is the classical finite Weyl character $\chi_\lambda$. It is universal among finite dimensional highest-label modules generated by a vector of label $\lambda$. It has a unique maximal proper submodule and unique simple head $L_\zeta(\lambda)$. The simple heads are pairwise nonisomorphic and exhaust finite dimensional simple type-1 modules. The dual Weyl module has the same character, unique simple socle $L_\zeta(\lambda)$, and weights at most $\lambda$.

These assertions use the inherited Axiom of Choice. They do not assert root-specialized semisimplicity or that these Weyl modules are simple.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Choice. For each dominant weight $\lambda$ there exists a unique indecomposable tilting module $T_\zeta(\lambda)$ with highest label $\lambda$. It has a normalized inclusion $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)\hookrightarrow T_\zeta(\lambda)$ with Weyl-filtered cokernel of strictly smaller labels and highest multiplicity one. Every tilting module is a finite direct sum of these. In every finite saturated truncation $\mathcal C_\Gamma$ one has
$$
M\text{ is dual-Weyl-filtered}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta_\zeta(\mu),M)=0\text{ for all }\mu\in\Gamma,
$$
and the dual Weyl-filtration criterion with the variables interchanged. No semisimplicity or alcove dimension assertion is included here.

Under [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], and the inherited Axiom of Choice, the tensor product of two Weyl-filtered modules is Weyl-filtered, and the tensor product of two dual-Weyl-filtered modules is dual-Weyl-filtered. Hence tilting modules are closed under tensor products, ordinary duals and finite direct sums, and contain the tensor unit. This theorem does not presume direct-summand closure or classify indecomposable tiltings.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For the actual root Weyl families of [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], Weyl-filtered and dual-Weyl-filtered modules are closed under direct summands. Hence tiltings are closed under direct summands, and each tilting is a finite direct sum of indecomposable tiltings. One has $\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_\zeta(\lambda),\nabla_\zeta(\mu))=\delta_{\lambda\mu}\mathbb C$ and every extension of a Weyl-filtered module by a dual-Weyl-filtered module splits. Every indecomposable tilting has a unique maximal label, of multiplicity one, and two indecomposable tiltings with the same maximal label are isomorphic. These assertions give uniqueness where the objects exist; they make no existence claim for an arbitrary prescribed label.

Use the full simply-laced weight lattice $P$, root lattice $Q$, parameter $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta^2)=\ell$ odd greater than $h$, and full type-1 category of [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]]. If $L_\zeta(\mu)$ is a composition factor of $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$, then $\mu\le\lambda$ and $\mu\in(W\ltimes\ell Q)\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda$. More generally every Weyl section and every composition factor of an indecomposable tilting module of highest label $\lambda$ has label in this same affine orbit. These claims hold for both possible orders $\ell$ and $2\ell$ of $\zeta$, with no coprimality condition on the index $[P:Q]$. They use the inherited Axiom of Choice.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Choice. Use the finite simply-laced full weight datum $P$, root lattice $Q$, positive roots $\Phi^+$ and root normalization $(\alpha,\alpha)=2$. Let $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta^2)=\ell$ be odd and greater than the Coxeter number. Both $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta)=\ell$ and $2\ell$ are allowed. Work in the full toral-weight Lusztig category of [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]].

Define $\eta\preceq_\ell\lambda$ to mean that $\eta+\rho$ is obtained from $\lambda+\rho$ by a finite sequence, possibly empty, of reflections
$$
r_{\alpha,k}(x)=x-((x,\alpha)-k\ell)\alpha,\qquad \alpha\in\Phi^+,\quad k\in\mathbb Z,
$$
where each step is strictly downward: $(x,\alpha)>k\ell$. Intermediate labels need not be dominant. Every composition label $\eta$ of $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$ or $\nabla_\zeta(\lambda)$ satisfies $\eta\preceq_\ell\lambda$. Every Weyl section and every composition label of the indecomposable tilting $T_\zeta(\lambda)$ also satisfies $\eta\preceq_\ell\lambda$.

Use [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], normalize every root to have squared length two, and use the pivot $g=K_{-2\rho^\vee}$ from [[thm-root-of-unity-lusztig-module-category-is-braided-rigid]]. With the inherited Axiom of Choice,
$$
\operatorname{qdim}\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)=\prod_{\alpha>0}\frac{[\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle]_\zeta}{[\langle\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle]_\zeta}.
$$
Every denominator is nonzero. Extend the displayed product to all integral $\lambda$. It is alternating under the dot action of $W$ and periodic under translation by $\ell Q$, hence satisfies $d(w\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda)=\det(w)d(\lambda)$ for the affine Weyl group $W_\ell=W\ltimes\ell Q$. Its zero set is exactly the affine singular weights. In particular all weights in the open bottom alcove have nonzero Weyl quantum dimension. Every Weyl-filtered module all of whose section labels are affine singular has quantum dimension zero. No assertion about arbitrary outside-alcove indecomposable tiltings is inferred without a proof about their actual section labels or their tensor-ideal generation.

In the selected simply-laced branch, if $\lambda\in P^+$ satisfies $\langle\lambda+\rho,\theta^\vee\rangle\le\ell$, then $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)=L_\zeta(\lambda)=T_\zeta(\lambda)=\nabla_\zeta(\lambda)$. Its quantum dimension is nonzero for strict inequality and zero for equality. Thus the boundary case is included, not inferred from an open-alcove statement. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the Weyl suppliers.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be an irreducible simply-laced root system, normalize roots to squared length two, and write $\theta=\sum a_i\alpha_i$, $h=1+\sum a_i$. Let $\ell>h$ be odd and $k=\ell-h$. Put $C=\{x:(x+\rho,\alpha_i)>0,\ (x+\rho,\theta)<\ell\}$. For every integral $\mu\in C$ and every facet $F$ of its closure, there is an integral point $\lambda$ in the relative interior of $F$ such that the ordinary Weyl-dominant representative $\gamma$ of $\mu-\lambda$ satisfies $\gamma\in P^+$ and $(\gamma,\theta)\le k+1$. Thus $\gamma$ is in the dominant part of the closed shifted bottom alcove. A finite facet point $\lambda$ need not be dominant before affine transport.

The assertion transports to every affine alcove. If the transported facet lies inside the strict shifted dominant chamber, the transported integral facet point is dominant. This is a geometric displacement assertion; it does not assert a tensor-summand or translation-functor conclusion.

For the finite coordinate verifications use the $E_8$ roots $\pm e_i\pm e_j$ and the half sums with an even number of minus signs, and simple vectors $\alpha_1=(e_1-e_2-e_3-e_4-e_5-e_6-e_7+e_8)/2$, $\alpha_2=e_1+e_2$, $\alpha_3=e_2-e_1$, $\alpha_j=e_{j-1}-e_{j-2}$ for $4\le j\le8$. The first six or seven give the $E_6,E_7$ subsystems.

Let $\Phi$ be a finite simply-laced root system in its real root span, with positive roots $\Phi^+$, root lattice $Q$, Weyl group $W$ and $(\alpha,\alpha)=2$. Let $\ell>0$ and $W_\ell=W\ltimes\ell Q$, acting by affine isometries on shifted coordinates. Its walls and reflections are
$$
H_{\alpha,k}=\{z:(z,\alpha)=k\ell\},\qquad r_{\alpha,k}(z)=z-((z,\alpha)-k\ell)\alpha.
$$
Let $C$ be an open alcove, $F$ one of its facets, $x$ in the relative interior of $F$, and $y\in C$. Write $s_F$ for the facet reflection. Then, for all $u,v\in W_\ell$,
$$
\|ux-vy\|\ge\|x-y\|.
$$
Equality holds exactly when $(ux,vy)=(\tau x,\tau y)$ for some $\tau\in W_\ell$. Equivalently, the regular orbit points at minimum distance from $gx$ are precisely $gy$ and $gs_Fy$.

Call $F$ a lower facet when, for its positive finite root $\alpha$, $C$ lies in $(z,\alpha)>k\ell$. Suppose it is lower and $x'=r_N\cdots r_1x$ is obtained by strict downward reflections: $r_j=r_{\alpha_j,k_j}$ with $\alpha_j\in\Phi^+$ and $(x_{j-1},\alpha_j)>k_j\ell$. Then every $y'\in W_\ell y$ satisfying $\|x'-y'\|\le\|x-y\|$ satisfies $y'\le y$ in root order, meaning $y-y'$ is a nonnegative real combination of positive roots. At integral weights with integer $\ell$, these are nonnegative integer root combinations. No dominance condition on the intermediate points is required. The result is choice free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the Weyl/global-basis suppliers. Work in the full-weight-lattice, simple simply-laced branch with odd $\ell>h$ and $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta^2)=\ell$, and use the actual Weyl families of [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]]. Let $\mathcal T_\zeta$ be the full category of finite-dimensional modules with both Weyl and dual-Weyl filtrations. Put $g=K_{-2\rho^\vee}$, $t_X(a)=\operatorname{Tr}_X(ga)$, and
$$\mathcal N(X,Y)=\{f:X\to Y:t_X(bf)=0\text{ for all }b:Y\to X\}.$$
Then $\mathcal N$ is a two-sided tensor ideal. The quotient $\mathcal T_\zeta/\mathcal N$, with the same objects and morphisms modulo $\mathcal N$, is an idempotent-complete semisimple braided rigid spherical category. Its simple objects are the isomorphism classes of indecomposable tiltings $T$ with $\operatorname{Tr}_T(g)\ne0$. The tensor unit is simple. If exactly finitely many such classes exist, the quotient is a fusion category. This theorem does not identify those classes with an alcove or assert their finiteness; that is the separate quantum-specific classification obligation.

Every $W$-orbit in $E$ has exactly one point in $\overline{\mathcal C}$. For $\eta\in\overline{\mathcal C}$, its stabilizer is generated by those simple reflections $s_i$ with $(\eta,\alpha_i)=0$. The group acts simply transitively on open chambers. There is a unique longest element $w_0$, characterized by $w_0\Phi^+=\Phi^-$; it has length $|\Phi^+|$ and satisfies $w_0^2=1$. In particular every weight orbit has a unique dominant weight. These assertions include rank zero and singular wall points, without AC.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a fixed
positive system. Then the maps
$$V\longmapsto\lambda(V),\qquad \lambda\longmapsto L(\lambda)$$
are mutually inverse bijections between the isomorphism classes of
finite-dimensional irreducible representations of $\mathfrak g$ and the
dominant integral weights
([[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]); here $\lambda(V)$
is the highest weight of $V$
([[def-highest-weight-vector-and-highest-weight-module]]) and $L(\lambda)$ is
the simple quotient of $M_{\mathrm{int}}(\lambda)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a chosen
positive system, and let $V$ be a representation generated by a highest weight
vector $v$ of weight $\lambda$
([[def-highest-weight-vector-and-highest-weight-module]]). Then
$$V=U(\mathfrak n^-)v=U(\mathfrak n^-)\mathbb Cv ,$$
every weight $\mu$ of $V$ is of the form
$\mu=\lambda-\sum_in_i\alpha_i$ with $n_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, so that
$\mu\le\lambda$ in the root order
([[def-partial-order-on-weights]]), and
$$V_\lambda=\mathbb Cv .$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $V$ be a
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$-module and let $W$ act on the
finite-support elements of the completed character ring $\mathcal R$ by
$w\cdot e^\mu=e^{w\mu}$ as in [[def-weyl-alternation-operator]]. Then
$$w\cdot\operatorname{ch}V=\operatorname{ch}V\qquad(w\in W),$$
and equivalently the weight multiplicities of $V$ satisfy
$\dim V_{w\mu}=\dim V_\mu$ for all $w\in W$ and $\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$, so
that $\operatorname{ch}V=\sum_\mu(\dim V_{w\mu})e^\mu$. In particular the
formal character of every finite-dimensional simple module is $W$-invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In the notation of
[[def-tensor-product-multiplicity-for-highest-weight-modules]], for all
$\lambda,\mu\in\Lambda^+$ the following hold in the completed character ring
$\mathcal R$ of [[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]]:

(i) $\operatorname{ch}(L(\lambda)\otimes L(\mu))=\sum_{\nu\in\Lambda^+}c^\nu_{\lambda\mu}\operatorname{ch}L(\nu)$,
a finite sum;
(ii) if $V$ is any finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$-module and
$\operatorname{ch}V=\sum_{\nu\in\Lambda^+}a_\nu\operatorname{ch}L(\nu)$ with
integers $a_\nu$ (finitely many nonzero), then $a_\nu=[V:L(\nu)]$ for every
$\nu$, so the expansion coefficients of the character are exactly the
composition multiplicities and the elements $\operatorname{ch}L(\nu)$,
$\nu\in\Lambda^+$, are linearly independent in $\mathcal R$;
(iii) for every weight $\gamma\in\mathfrak h^*$ one has the weight-multiplicity
formula
$$\dim\bigl(L(\lambda)\otimes L(\mu)\bigr)_\gamma=\sum_{\sigma+\tau=\gamma}m_\lambda(\sigma)m_\mu(\tau),$$
a finite sum, where $m_\lambda(\sigma)=\dim L(\lambda)_\sigma$ and
$m_\mu(\tau)=\dim L(\mu)_\tau$
([[def-formal-character-of-a-finite-dimensional-weight-module]],
[[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For all dominant integral weights
$\lambda,\mu,\nu\in\Lambda^+$ the tensor-product multiplicity of
[[def-tensor-product-multiplicity-for-highest-weight-modules]] is
$$c^\nu_{\lambda\mu}=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}\,m_\mu\bigl(w(\nu+\rho)-(\lambda+\rho)\bigr),$$
where $m_\mu(\sigma)=\dim L(\mu)_\sigma$ is the weight multiplicity
([[def-formal-character-of-a-finite-dimensional-weight-module]]) and $W$ is
the Weyl group with length function $\ell$; only finitely many summands are
nonzero. Equivalently, after the substitution $w\mapsto w^{-1}$ and
Weyl-invariance of the weight multiplicities
([[prop-characters-of-finite-dimensional-modules-are-weyl-invariant]]),
$$c^\nu_{\lambda\mu}=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}\,m_\mu\bigl(\nu+\rho-w(\lambda+\rho)\bigr).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Every weight $\eta$ of $L(\gamma)$ has norm at most $\|\gamma\|$. Indeed its dominant Weyl conjugate $\eta^+$ is a weight by [F6], so $\beta=\gamma-\eta^+\in Q_+$. Then $\|\gamma\|^2-\|\eta^+\|^2=(\beta,\gamma+\eta^+)\ge0$, by dominance of both labels. Every extremal weight $w\gamma$ has multiplicity one, by Weyl invariance and the one-dimensional highest line. Also, if $L(b)$ occurs in $L(a)\otimes L(\gamma)$, then $b-a$ is a weight of $L(\gamma)$. To prove this last assertion, project a highest vector to first-factor weight spaces, and take a maximal first weight $\eta$ in its support. For each simple raising operator its first-factor contribution at $\eta+\alpha_i$ cannot cancel a second-factor contribution, because that first weight is absent. Thus the component at $\eta$ lies in the simultaneous raising kernel in the first factor. Simplicity of $L(a)$ makes that kernel precisely its highest line: any other highest vector would generate a proper highest submodule. Consequently $\eta=a$, and the highest vector has nonzero projection to $L(a)_a\otimes L(\gamma)_{b-a}$. This proves the assertion and the tensor bound $\|b-a\|\le\|\gamma\|$.

Suppose $\mu$ is regular and outside the bottom alcove, and put $y=\mu+\rho$. Its alcove $C$ is inside the strict finite dominant chamber. Choose a point $p$ in the bottom alcove, sufficiently close to a small positive multiple of $\rho$, so that $(p,\alpha)<\ell$ for every positive root. Perturb $p$ within that open set so that the segment from $p$ to the regular point $y$ crosses no codimension-two intersection of walls. Such a perturbation exists because only finitely many walls meet the bounded segment neighborhood, and each forbidden intersection imposes a proper affine condition on $p$. The segment stays in the strict dominant chamber by convexity and crosses at least one wall because $C$ is not the bottom alcove. Its last crossing enters $C$ through a facet $F$. A crossed wall has positive-root equation $(z,\alpha)=m\ell$ with $m\ge1$; the linear pairing on the segment crosses this level upwards, since its initial value is below $\ell$. Thus $F$ is a lower facet of $C$. Its relative interior is internal to the strict dominant chamber: it is a facet of an alcove in that chamber and is not one of the finite chamber walls.

Apply [F4] to choose a dominant integral label $\lambda$ with $x=\lambda+\rho$ in the relative interior of $F$, and with $\gamma$ the ordinary dominant representative of $\mu-\lambda$ in the closed bottom alcove. Put $\delta=\mu-\lambda\in W\gamma$, so $\|x-y\|=\|\gamma\|$. By [F3], $\Delta_\zeta(\gamma)$ is tilting. The tensor $M=T_\zeta(\lambda)\otimes\Delta_\zeta(\gamma)$ is therefore tilting by [F1]. The label $\lambda$ is affine singular. Every Weyl section of $T_\zeta(\lambda)$ is singular by [F2] and has zero dimension by [F3]. Additivity gives $d_{T_\zeta(\lambda)}=0$, so its identity, and then $1_M$, are negligible by [F5].

The classical multiplicity of $L(\mu)$ in $L(\lambda)\otimes L(\gamma)$ is one. The Racah formula of [F6] is $$c^\mu_{\lambda\gamma}=\sum_{v\in W}\det(v)\dim L(\gamma)_{v(y)-x}.$$ The identity term equals one since $y-x=\delta\in W\gamma$, by step 1.1. For $v\ne1$, strict finite dominance of both $x$ and $y$ gives $(x,y-vy)>0$: $y-vy$ is a nonzero nonnegative root combination, as follows by a reduced reflection word from the dominant $y$. Hence $\|vy-x\|^2-\|y-x\|^2=2(x,y-vy)>0$. Step 1.1 makes the other weight multiplicities zero. This proves the claimed coefficient without assuming that every extremal tensor label occurs.

Let $\lambda'$ be a Weyl section label of $T_\zeta(\lambda)$, and suppose a classical tensor constituent $L(
u)$ occurs in $L(\lambda')\otimes L(\gamma)$ with $
u$ in the affine dot orbit of $\mu$. Put $x'=\lambda'+ho$, $y'=
u+ho$. Step 1.1 gives $\|y'-x'\|\le\|\gamma\|=\|y-x\|$. By [F2], $x'$ is obtained from $x$ by a downward chain. The lower-facet conclusion of [F4] therefore gives $
u\le\mu$. If $
u=\mu$, the closest-pair equality case provides a common affine isometry $	au$ with $(x',y)=(	au x,	au y)$. Regularity of $y$ forces $	au=1$, so $\lambda'=\lambda$. Weyl flags tensor to Weyl flags and their section multiplicities are exactly the classical coefficients by [F1] and [F6]. The top $\lambda$ occurs once in $T_\zeta(\lambda)$; step 3.1 and the exclusion just proved imply $(M:\Delta_\zeta(\mu))=1$, and no Weyl section in the $\mu$ orbit is strictly above $\mu$.

Decompose $M$ into indecomposable tiltings by [F1]. Its $\mu$ Weyl section belongs to some $T_\zeta(\tau)$. This forces $\tau\ge\mu$ by highest-weight dominance and places $\tau$ in the same affine orbit by [F2]. The last assertion of step 4.1 forces $\tau=\mu$. Thus $T_\zeta(\mu)$ is a direct summand of the negligible object $M$, and its identity is negligible by composing $1_M$ with the inclusion and projection. Its dimension is zero by [F5]. If $\mu$ is singular instead, [F2] and [F3] directly give dimension zero for all its Weyl sections, hence for $T_\zeta(\mu)$, and [F5] applies. This covers every label outside $A_\ell$, including its upper boundary. For labels inside $A_\ell$ the final assertion is exactly [F3].

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the integral global-basis suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a finite simply-laced root system, its full weight lattice $P$ and coroot lattice $Q^\vee$, and the corresponding Lusztig form $U_A$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$. Let $\zeta\in\mathbb C^\times$ satisfy $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta^2)=\ell$, with $\ell$ odd and $\ell>h$, where $h$ is the Coxeter number. Both orders $\ell$ and $2\ell$ for $\zeta$ are permitted. Work in the category of finite dimensional integrable type-1 modules with full toral quantum-binomial weight characters supplied by [[thm-root-of-unity-lusztig-module-category-is-braided-rigid]], not just eigenvalues of the $K_i$.

For $\lambda\in P^+$ let $V_A(\lambda)=U_A^-v_\lambda$ be the actual finite free highest lattice of [[thm-quantum-highest-weight-modules-deform-the-classical-weight-character]]. Define
$$
\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)=\mathbb C\otimes_{A,\,v\mapsto\zeta}V_A(\lambda),\qquad \nabla_\zeta(\lambda)=\Delta_\zeta(-w_0\lambda)^*.
$$
Here $(-)^*$ is the ordinary finite-dimensional Hopf dual in the stated category. These are the **Weyl** and **dual Weyl** families. The pivotal isomorphism identifies their double duals with the original modules, so ordinary duality exchanges the two families, with label $\lambda\mapsto-w_0\lambda$.

A module has a Weyl or dual Weyl filtration if it has a finite submodule filtration with sections in the corresponding family. A **tilting module** has both filtrations. Existence of indecomposable tiltings at every label, their classification, and their affine-alcove behavior are separate results; these are not included in this definition.

Under [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$ is a nonzero finite dimensional integrable type-1 module, cyclic on a highest vector of label $\lambda$ with one-dimensional highest space. Its formal character is the classical finite Weyl character $\chi_\lambda$. It is universal among finite dimensional highest-label modules generated by a vector of label $\lambda$. It has a unique maximal proper submodule and unique simple head $L_\zeta(\lambda)$. The simple heads are pairwise nonisomorphic and exhaust finite dimensional simple type-1 modules. The dual Weyl module has the same character, unique simple socle $L_\zeta(\lambda)$, and weights at most $\lambda$.

These assertions use the inherited Axiom of Choice. They do not assert root-specialized semisimplicity or that these Weyl modules are simple.

Under [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], and the inherited Axiom of Choice, the tensor product of two Weyl-filtered modules is Weyl-filtered, and the tensor product of two dual-Weyl-filtered modules is dual-Weyl-filtered. Hence tilting modules are closed under tensor products, ordinary duals and finite direct sums, and contain the tensor unit. This theorem does not presume direct-summand closure or classify indecomposable tiltings.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For the actual root Weyl families of [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], Weyl-filtered and dual-Weyl-filtered modules are closed under direct summands. Hence tiltings are closed under direct summands, and each tilting is a finite direct sum of indecomposable tiltings. One has $\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_\zeta(\lambda),\nabla_\zeta(\mu))=\delta_{\lambda\mu}\mathbb C$ and every extension of a Weyl-filtered module by a dual-Weyl-filtered module splits. Every indecomposable tilting has a unique maximal label, of multiplicity one, and two indecomposable tiltings with the same maximal label are isomorphic. These assertions give uniqueness where the objects exist; they make no existence claim for an arbitrary prescribed label.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Choice. For each dominant weight $\lambda$ there exists a unique indecomposable tilting module $T_\zeta(\lambda)$ with highest label $\lambda$. It has a normalized inclusion $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)\hookrightarrow T_\zeta(\lambda)$ with Weyl-filtered cokernel of strictly smaller labels and highest multiplicity one. Every tilting module is a finite direct sum of these. In every finite saturated truncation $\mathcal C_\Gamma$ one has
$$
M\text{ is dual-Weyl-filtered}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta_\zeta(\mu),M)=0\text{ for all }\mu\in\Gamma,
$$
and the dual Weyl-filtration criterion with the variables interchanged. No semisimplicity or alcove dimension assertion is included here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the Weyl/global-basis suppliers. Work in the full-weight-lattice, simple simply-laced branch with odd $\ell>h$ and $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta^2)=\ell$, and use the actual Weyl families of [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]]. Let $\mathcal T_\zeta$ be the full category of finite-dimensional modules with both Weyl and dual-Weyl filtrations. Put $g=K_{-2\rho^\vee}$, $t_X(a)=\operatorname{Tr}_X(ga)$, and
$$\mathcal N(X,Y)=\{f:X\to Y:t_X(bf)=0\text{ for all }b:Y\to X\}.$$
Then $\mathcal N$ is a two-sided tensor ideal. The quotient $\mathcal T_\zeta/\mathcal N$, with the same objects and morphisms modulo $\mathcal N$, is an idempotent-complete semisimple braided rigid spherical category. Its simple objects are the isomorphism classes of indecomposable tiltings $T$ with $\operatorname{Tr}_T(g)\ne0$. The tensor unit is simple. If exactly finitely many such classes exist, the quotient is a fusion category. This theorem does not identify those classes with an alcove or assert their finiteness; that is the separate quantum-specific classification obligation.

Work with the full weight lattice of a simple simply-laced root system, roots of squared length two, odd $\ell>h$, and $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta^2)=\ell$ in the actual full toral-weight Lusztig category. Allow both $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta)=\ell$ and $2\ell$. Put
$$A_\ell=\{
u\in P^+:(

For every dominant $\mu
otin A_\ell$, the indecomposable tilting $T_\zeta(\mu)$ has zero quantum dimension and negligible identity morphism. For every $

Use the full simply-laced weight lattice $P$, root lattice $Q$, parameter $\operatorname{ord}(\zeta^2)=\ell$ odd greater than $h$, and full type-1 category of [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]]. If $L_\zeta(\mu)$ is a composition factor of $\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)$, then $\mu\le\lambda$ and $\mu\in(W\ltimes\ell Q)\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda$. More generally every Weyl section and every composition factor of an indecomposable tilting module of highest label $\lambda$ has label in this same affine orbit. These claims hold for both possible orders $\ell$ and $2\ell$ of $\zeta$, with no coprimality condition on the index $[P:Q]$. They use the inherited Axiom of Choice.

Use [[def-root-of-unity-weyl-and-dual-weyl-module-families]], normalize every root to have squared length two, and use the pivot $g=K_{-2\rho^\vee}$ from [[thm-root-of-unity-lusztig-module-category-is-braided-rigid]]. With the inherited Axiom of Choice,
$$
\operatorname{qdim}\Delta_\zeta(\lambda)=\prod_{\alpha>0}\frac{[\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle]_\zeta}{[\langle\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle]_\zeta}.
$$
Every denominator is nonzero. Extend the displayed product to all integral $\lambda$. It is alternating under the dot action of $W$ and periodic under translation by $\ell Q$, hence satisfies $d(w\mathbin{\cdot}\lambda)=\det(w)d(\lambda)$ for the affine Weyl group $W_\ell=W\ltimes\ell Q$. Its zero set is exactly the affine singular weights. In particular all weights in the open bottom alcove have nonzero Weyl quantum dimension. Every Weyl-filtered module all of whose section labels are affine singular has quantum dimension zero. No assertion about arbitrary outside-alcove indecomposable tiltings is inferred without a proof about their actual section labels or their tensor-ideal generation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In the notation of
[[def-tensor-product-multiplicity-for-highest-weight-modules]], for all
$\lambda,\mu\in\Lambda^+$ the following hold in the completed character ring
$\mathcal R$ of [[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]]:

(i) $\operatorname{ch}(L(\lambda)\otimes L(\mu))=\sum_{\nu\in\Lambda^+}c^\nu_{\lambda\mu}\operatorname{ch}L(\nu)$,
a finite sum;
(ii) if $V$ is any finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$-module and
$\operatorname{ch}V=\sum_{\nu\in\Lambda^+}a_\nu\operatorname{ch}L(\nu)$ with
integers $a_\nu$ (finitely many nonzero), then $a_\nu=[V:L(\nu)]$ for every
$\nu$, so the expansion coefficients of the character are exactly the
composition multiplicities and the elements $\operatorname{ch}L(\nu)$,
$\nu\in\Lambda^+$, are linearly independent in $\mathcal R$;
(iii) for every weight $\gamma\in\mathfrak h^*$ one has the weight-multiplicity
formula
$$\dim\bigl(L(\lambda)\otimes L(\mu)\bigr)_\gamma=\sum_{\sigma+\tau=\gamma}m_\lambda(\sigma)m_\mu(\tau),$$
a finite sum, where $m_\lambda(\sigma)=\dim L(\lambda)_\sigma$ and
$m_\mu(\tau)=\dim L(\mu)_\tau$
([[def-formal-character-of-a-finite-dimensional-weight-module]],
[[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For all dominant integral weights
$\lambda,\mu,\nu\in\Lambda^+$ the tensor-product multiplicity of
[[def-tensor-product-multiplicity-for-highest-weight-modules]] is
$$c^\nu_{\lambda\mu}=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}\,m_\mu\bigl(w(\nu+\rho)-(\lambda+\rho)\bigr),$$
where $m_\mu(\sigma)=\dim L(\mu)_\sigma$ is the weight multiplicity
([[def-formal-character-of-a-finite-dimensional-weight-module]]) and $W$ is
the Weyl group with length function $\ell$; only finitely many summands are
nonzero. Equivalently, after the substitution $w\mapsto w^{-1}$ and
Weyl-invariance of the weight multiplicities
([[prop-characters-of-finite-dimensional-modules-are-weyl-invariant]]),
$$c^\nu_{\lambda\mu}=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}\,m_\mu\bigl(\nu+\rho-w(\lambda+\rho)\bigr).$$

Use the affine-wall notation and componentwise fundamental alcove $A$ from [[def-cg-affine-root-hyperplane-reflection-and-alcove]] and [[lem-cg-highest-root-and-fundamental-alcove]]. Let $J$ be the affine facet-type set from [[lem-cg-affine-alcove-separation-and-facet-types]], with one label $0_i$ for each nonempty irreducible component, and let $s_a$ be the reflection in the fundamental facet of type $a\in J$. Let $W_{\rm abs}$, its Coxeter matrix $m_{ab}=\operatorname{ord}(s_as_b)$, and $\varphi:W_{\rm abs}\to W_a$ be those of [[lem-cg-affine-generic-gallery-paths-and-disk-moves]]; its finite labels are $2,3,4,6$, and $m_{ab}=\infty$ only for the two opposite facets of a rank-one component. If $J=\varnothing$, take $W_{\rm abs}=W_a=\{1\}$.

**(1) Transitivity and generation.** The subgroup $G:=\langle s_a:a\in J\rangle\le W_a$ equals $W_a$, and $W_a$ acts transitively on the set of alcoves. Every affine wall supports a facet of the closure of some alcove; if $H$ is a facet wall of $g(A)$, its reflection is $g s_a g^{-1}$ for the type $a$ of that facet.

**(2) Presentation and simple transitivity.** The homomorphism $\varphi:W_{\rm abs}\to W_a$ is an isomorphism. Thus $W_a$ is the Coxeter group with simple system $(s_a)_{a\in J}$, and it acts simply transitively on alcoves: for any two alcoves $C,C'$ there is exactly one $g\in W_a$ such that $g(C)=C'$.

**(3) Length.** Let $\ell(g)$ be the minimum number of facet reflections from $(s_a)_{a\in J}$ whose product is $g$. For every $g\in W_a$,
$$\ell(g)=\#\operatorname{Sep}(A,g(A)),$$
where $\operatorname{Sep}$ is the separating-wall set of [[lem-cg-affine-alcove-separation-and-facet-types]]. A straight generic segment between interior points of $A$ and $g(A)$ crosses each separating wall exactly once and gives a gallery attaining the minimum. The argument includes rank-one factors and reducible systems with the product conventions of [[lem-cg-highest-root-and-fundamental-alcove]] (3).

**(4) Comparison.** The finite root-system types are the standard crystallographic types $A_n,B_n,C_n,D_n,E_6,E_7,E_8,F_4,G_2$ (with the low-rank identifications in [[thm-classification-of-irreducible-reduced-crystallographic-root-systems]]). In that root-system normalization, $W_a=Q^\vee\rtimes W$ from [[lem-cg-affine-reflection-identities-and-local-finiteness]] is the standard affine Weyl group. This does not identify it with an untwisted Kac–Moody loop realization, and it does not assert that the extended group $P^\vee\rtimes W$ is a Coxeter group with the same simple system. No axiom of choice is used.

Every $W$-orbit in $E$ has exactly one point in $\overline{\mathcal C}$. For $\eta\in\overline{\mathcal C}$, its stabilizer is generated by those simple reflections $s_i$ with $(\eta,\alpha_i)=0$. The group acts simply transitively on open chambers. There is a unique longest element $w_0$, characterized by $w_0\Phi^+=\Phi^-$; it has length $|\Phi^+|$ and satisfies $w_0^2=1$. In particular every weight orbit has a unique dominant weight. These assertions include rank zero and singular wall points, without AC.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
